title: Why Your Retail CPG AI Forecasting Pilot Stalls At Day 60
description: Three data gaps kill a CPG AI forecasting pilot before day 60: shipments read as demand, a SKU master that churned, net revenue nobody traced.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: What a CPG AI forecasting pilot needs that a shipment-only dataset cannot give it: weekly POS, a stable SKU master, and a net-of-returns revenue signal
answer: An AI forecasting pilot stalls when the data feeding the model does not describe demand. Three failures account for most of it: shipment data substituted for POS, a SKU master that turned over during the training window, and gross-ship numbers that ignore returns and deduction leakage. The model is not wrong. The signal is.
answerQualifier: Based on McKinsey research on digital pilot purgatory, McKinsey's State of Food and Beverage data on new-item share of sales at mid-market CPG, Overdeduct and Inmar benchmarks on retail-deduction load, practitioner commentary from TrueGradient and Impact Analytics on AI-forecasting data quality, the bullwhip-effect research from Hau Lee et al. in Sloan Management Review, and public retailer data programs (Walmart Luminate, Amazon Vendor Central). October 2026.

faq.q: Why does an AI forecasting pilot miss on exactly the SKUs that matter most?
faq.a: The pilot usually misses on your fastest movers and your promoted SKUs. Both share a data gap. A fast mover with a recent stockout trains the model on a demand number lower than real demand. A promoted SKU with no flag in the data trains the model on a baseline inflated by lift. Both failures look like model error on the dashboard. Both are data problems upstream of the model.

faq.q: Can I run an AI forecasting pilot on shipment history alone?
faq.a: You can run it. The model will fit the shipment pattern. The forecast will miss sell-through turns by whatever time it takes the retailer to reorder, which is one to four weeks for most CPG categories. Pilots run on shipment-only data commonly show acceptable in-sample accuracy during training and lose it when the retailer's order cadence shifts. If you have access to Walmart Luminate, Target Mindset, or Amazon Vendor Central POS, pull it before the pilot starts.

faq.q: How much SKU turnover is too much for a forecasting pilot?
faq.a: McKinsey's State of Food and Beverage data shows new items drive 19 percent of sales at CPG suppliers in the $100 million to $500 million band, which implies continuous SKU addition and retirement in the training window. A pilot that treats a replaced SKU as new, and the retired one as discontinued, splits what is often one continuous demand pattern into two shorter and noisier ones. Document the SKU-replacement map before training. One field linking a new SKU to the one it replaces recovers most of the lost signal.

faq.q: Why do my gross shipments not reconcile to my collected revenue?
faq.a: A CPG supplier commonly collects less than the gross shipment value after returns, deduction leakage, and reserve adjustments. Industry benchmarks from Overdeduct and Inmar put deductions and chargebacks at 2 to 15 percent of gross sales across CPG, with mid-market suppliers writing off 1.2 to 2.4 percent of gross revenue each year on unrecovered deductions alone. A forecasting model trained on gross-ship numbers forecasts volume you will not keep. Pull the net number from your AR aging or deduction register and train on that.

faq.q: What should I audit before I commit to an AI forecasting pilot?
faq.a: Audit three things first. The demand signal (POS or shipment, weekly or monthly, which retailers provide what). The SKU master history (how many SKUs added, retired, or renumbered in the last 24 months, with a replacement map). And the net-revenue reconciliation (gross ships minus returns minus deductions). All three live in systems you own today. None require the pilot vendor's platform to run.

title: The Amazon 1P Termination Notice: What 30 Days Actually Buys You
description: An Amazon 1P termination email arrives with 30 to 60 days notice. What happens to open POs, pending claims, and the audit posture that would have caught it earlier.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Amazon 1P vendor termination notice: the 90 days of data that predicted it and the audit posture that would have caught it earlier
answer: Amazon's 1P termination notice usually gives 30 to 60 days before purchase orders stop, and the decision is almost always algorithmic once it lands. Community operators report the cut is driven by contribution margin and Net PPM, not by revenue alone. A 42% Net PPM account can be terminated if its category is competitive. Open shortage claims stay disputable inside the notice window, and your audit posture is the single lever left.
answerQualifier: Based on r/VendorCentral community operators reporting terminations across US and EU accounts in Q2 to Q3 2026, plus public Amazon Vendor Central program guidance, September 2026. Amazon does not publish termination thresholds, so treat the specific figures below as vendor-reported patterns rather than policy.

faq.q: How much notice does Amazon give before terminating a 1P vendor account?
faq.a: Community operators on r/VendorCentral report notice periods running 30 to 60 days, occasionally two months, before Amazon stops issuing purchase orders. Some accounts get an intermediate ramp-down where PO volume drops sharply before the final cut. The termination email itself names the effective date and the last PO window. Amazon does not publish a standard notice period, so treat any figure as a data point, not a rule.

faq.q: Can you appeal an Amazon 1P vendor termination?
faq.a: Rarely, and only when the decision was algorithmic rather than a Vendor Manager judgment. One recovery operator on r/VendorCentral put it plainly: it is a set decision unless you were part of an algorithmic decision and still have contact with a Vendor Manager willing to work with you, because a VM is the only role that can override the system. If a VM already flagged your account as unwilling to work on Net PPM, the appeal path is effectively closed.

faq.q: What criteria triggers an Amazon 1P vendor termination?
faq.a: Vendor Managers who spoke on r/VendorCentral describe two main criteria: contribution margin for Amazon and Net PPM trend. Revenue alone does not protect an account. One operator reported a 42% Net PPM account was terminated because its category was highly competitive with many direct substitute vendors. Under-10M annual revenue accounts are reportedly a common target in the current wave. Amazon does not publish the thresholds.

faq.q: What happens to open shortage claims after a 1P termination notice?
faq.a: Open shortage and chargeback disputes stay in Vendor Central through the notice window and remain disputable under Amazon's normal rules. The 30-day dispute deadline from the chargeback notification still applies. Any credit that posts before the account closes goes through the final remittance cycle. Anything filed but unresolved at closure may need to be pursued through Amazon's post-termination case queue, which multiple operators report is slower and less responsive.

faq.q: Should you move to 3P selling after a 1P termination?
faq.a: Community operators are split. One vendor on r/VendorCentral reported moving to a 1P distributor and calling it a simplification. Another countered that the switch surrenders margin and brand control. The right answer depends on your category, your Net PPM at Amazon's shelf price, your non-Amazon revenue mix, and whether your brand carries independent demand. Talk to at least two operators who have made the transition in your category before deciding.

title: Amazon Marked Your Shortage Claim Closed. Was It Actually Paid?
description: A closed shortage claim in Vendor Central does not always mean the money came back. Three failure modes suppliers miss, and the 90-day re-audit that catches them.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Auditing closed Amazon shortage claims: Vendor Central status versus what actually posted to the remittance
answer: Amazon marks a shortage claim closed when it exits the workflow, not when a credit posts to your remittance. Three failure modes leak money past a closed status: no offsetting credit, multi-PO shortages split across claim IDs, and a post-close dispute path most vendors miss. A 90-day re-audit is the highest-ROI hour of the quarter.
answerQualifier: Based on public Amazon Vendor Central documentation, SPS Commerce and Inmar deduction benchmarks, and community-reported patterns from 1P suppliers, September 2026. Amazon's specific dispute-window language changes periodically. Confirm current windows in your own Vendor Central case portal before writing off a claim.

faq.q: What does closed mean in Amazon Vendor Central?
faq.a: Closed means the shortage claim has exited Amazon's active workflow. The claim ID stops appearing in your open-cases queue. It does not confirm that an offsetting credit posted to your remittance. Closed is a workflow status, not a payment status. Cross-check every closed claim against remittance detail before writing it off.

faq.q: Can you dispute an Amazon shortage claim after it's closed?
faq.a: Sometimes, but the mechanism changed in 2025. Amazon retired the older support-case path, and the current workflow gives you two chances only: the traditional dispute in Vendor Central, and a re-dispute if the first is denied. Community operators report the re-dispute now routes through a Contact Us case to a Tier 2 team, not the default Dispute Management button. Waiting 35 days after invoice due date before the first dispute is a widely-reported best practice.

faq.q: How do multi-PO shortages get split across claim IDs?
faq.a: When one physical shipment covers multiple POs and the receiver books shortages against each PO independently, Amazon can generate one claim ID per PO. If two claims reference the same missing units from opposite sides, only one may get resolved. The other stays open, expires, or closes without payment. Look for related claim IDs before writing off any single closed claim.

faq.q: Is a re-audit of closed shortage claims worth the time?
faq.a: For most 1P suppliers, yes. SPS Commerce reports that suppliers dispute only 20 to 30 percent of deductions to begin with, which leaves most closed claims unaudited. A 90-day re-audit catches the three failure modes below without needing new software. One finance analyst, one afternoon, and the remittance detail is enough to find the pattern if it's there.

faq.q: What evidence do I need before reopening a closed claim?
faq.a: Match every closed claim to its remittance line. Pull the ASN transmission timestamp, the proof of delivery signed by the receiver, and any related claim IDs on the same PO. If the offsetting credit is missing on the remittance, or if the closed claim references units also disputed under a different open claim, you have grounds to reopen. Amazon reviews reopens on documentation, not on the reopen request alone.

title: Net PPM vs. Contribution Margin: How Amazon Scores Your Profitability
description: What Net PPM, Contribution Margin, and CMLF measure, which one your vendor manager watches, and how to use all three before Annual Vendor Negotiations.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Whiteboard diagram comparing Net PPM, Contribution Margin, and CMLF as three layers of Amazon vendor profitability
answer: Net PPM (Net Pure Product Margin) is the metric your vendor manager watches. It measures Amazon's per-ASIN profit as a percentage of shipped revenue, and it drives Buy Box eligibility, PO volume, and the co-op ask at Annual Vendor Negotiations. Contribution Margin layers in Amazon's own variable costs (fulfillment, shipping, storage) and is Amazon's internal P&L view you rarely see. CMLF (likely Contribution Margin Less Funding) appears in vendor community discussions but has no confirmed public definition from Amazon.
answerQualifier: Based on the Net PPM formula documented by Amalytix and iNymbus, Contribution Margin definitions from Calbridge Analytics and MerchantSpring, category benchmarks from MerchantSpring and SmartScout, and vendor community discussion on r/VendorCentral. October 2026.

faq.q: What is Net PPM and how does Amazon calculate it?
faq.a: Net PPM stands for Net Pure Product Margin. It is Amazon's per-ASIN profit metric for 1P vendors. The formula, per Amalytix and iNymbus: (Shipped Revenue - Shipped COGS + Vendor Terms - Sales Discount) / Shipped Revenue. Vendor Terms includes co-op accruals, damage allowances, and freight allowances. Every dollar you fund into those terms lifts Amazon's calculated Net PPM on your catalog.

faq.q: What is Contribution Margin on Amazon and how is it different from Net PPM?
faq.a: Contribution Margin is Amazon's internal profitability view that layers variable costs on top of Net PPM. It subtracts fulfillment, shipping, storage, and customer service costs from the product margin. Vendors rarely see Contribution Margin directly. Net PPM is the metric that appears in your Vendor Central reports and drives the AVN conversation.

faq.q: What does CMLF stand for in Amazon vendor discussions?
faq.a: CMLF appears in r/VendorCentral threads but has no confirmed public definition from Amazon. Vendor community consensus suggests it stands for Contribution Margin Less Funding, meaning Contribution Margin after subtracting the co-op and marketing allowances vendors pay. Ask your vendor manager to define the term if it appears in your negotiation materials.

faq.q: What is a good Net PPM for Amazon vendors?
faq.a: Category benchmarks from MerchantSpring: hardlines 40 to 45%, softlines 30 to 37%, consumables 27 to 35%. Amazon's internal target for your catalog depends on your category average and your negotiation history. Pull your Net PPM report from Vendor Central at the ASIN level to see where you stand.

faq.q: What happens when my Net PPM drops below Amazon's target?
faq.a: Amazon may reduce PO volume, restrict advertising eligibility, or flag the ASIN as CRaP (Can't Realize a Profit). At AVN, the vendor manager opens with a margin headwind claim and asks for a higher co-op accrual rate. A sustained Net PPM shortfall is one of the trajectories that can end in a 1P termination notice.

title: One Bad ASN, Five Chargebacks on the Same Shipment
description: A single EDI 856 error on one shipment triggers ASN accuracy, shortage, OTIF, routing, and invoice chargebacks. The prevention step for each.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: One shipment branching into five chargeback types: ASN accuracy, shortage, OTIF, routing, and invoice mismatch
answer: A single bad EDI 856 ASN can trigger five separate chargebacks from one shipment: ASN accuracy, shortage, OTIF, routing or appointment exception, and invoice mismatch. Each chargeback has its own code and dispute path, but they share one root cause. Fixing them as five separate events misses the pattern is like playing whack a mole. Fixing the root cause ASN process closes all five.
answerQualifier: Based on public EDI and compliance documentation from SPS Commerce, Orderful, BOLD VAN, Inmar, and Consulterce, September 2026. Fee percentages are vendor-reported and vary by retailer and program update.

faq.q: Can one shipment really generate five separate chargebacks?
faq.a: Yes. A late or inaccurate ASN touches five different compliance categories because the 856 is the document that connects PO fulfillment, warehouse shipment, carrier appointment, retailer receiving, and invoicing. When the ASN is wrong, every system downstream records a different version of the same error, and each version gets its own chargeback code.

faq.q: What is the most common ASN error that triggers multiple chargebacks?
faq.a: A carton-count change after ASN generation. The warehouse adjusts the physical shipment, but the already-transmitted 856 carries the original count. The retailer receives a quantity that doesn't match the ASN, which triggers an ASN accuracy chargeback and a shortage claim. If the pick change also delayed the shipment, an OTIF miss follows.

faq.q: How do I know if my deductions share a single root cause?
faq.a: Pull five recent deductions and trace them back to the PO number. If two or more chargebacks on the same remittance point to the same PO, they likely started from one shipment failure. The evidence pack for that PO will show where the chain broke.

faq.q: Does fixing the ASN process actually reduce chargebacks from other categories?
faq.a: It reduces every chargeback category that depends on the ASN being accurate and on time: shortage claims that started as a count mismatch, OTIF misses that started as a late transmission, and invoice mismatches where the 810 followed the wrong ASN quantity. BOLD VAN reports that focused remediation targeting top chargeback categories reduces chargeback volume by 50 to 80% within one to two quarters.

title: The Five Business Central Settings Driving Retailer Deductions
description: Five Business Central EDI failure modes that end as retailer deductions: item references, unit of measure, posting timing, and ship-to mapping.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Business Central EDI 856 ASN failures
answer: Business Central generates no X12 EDI on its own, so every retailer ASN passes through a connector reading BC records. Five gaps corrupt it before transmission: missing item references, a wrong Qty. per Unit of Measure, a trigger wired to the wrong warehouse posting step, an unmapped ship-to or GLN, and kits that never explode to pack level.
answerQualifier: Based on Microsoft Learn documentation for Dynamics 365 Business Central covering item references, item units of measure, outbound warehouse flow, the Ship-to Address table, and assembly items, August 2026. Business Central's own fields and behavior are documented. Which validations a given EDI connector runs before transmission varies by vendor and is not a public standard.

faq.q: Does Business Central handle EDI natively?
faq.a: No. Business Central ships with a Data Exchange Framework and support for PEPPOL electronic invoices, which is a European e-invoicing standard, not retail X12. For a Walmart or Target ASN you need a connector or middleware layer that reads Business Central records and translates them into X12. That translation layer is where most retail EDI configuration actually lives.

faq.q: Why does a unit-of-measure setting cause a shortage deduction?
faq.a: The Qty. per Unit of Measure field on an item's alternate unit tells Business Central how many base units a case contains. If your ASN declares eaches where the retailer's implementation guide expects cases, your reported quantity is off by exactly the case-pack multiplier. The receiving count then reads short or over, and a short read becomes a shortage deduction.

faq.q: When should the ASN transmit relative to Business Central's warehouse posting?
faq.a: After the pick is registered and the shipment is posted, not before. In an advanced warehouse configuration, a registered warehouse pick updates Qty. Picked but does not post the shipment, so an ASN fired at pick registration describes intended quantities rather than confirmed ones. Posting the warehouse shipment is the event that reflects what actually left.

faq.q: What is the GLN field on a Business Central ship-to address for?
faq.a: GLN is the Global Location Number, a 13-character GS1 identifier for a physical location. Retailers use it to identify the receiving DC on EDI documents. Business Central has a dedicated GLN field on the Ship-to Address table, and leaving it blank forces your connector to derive the DC identity some other way, usually from a mapping table maintained by hand and updated late when a retailer opens a new facility.

faq.q: Do I need to replace Business Central to fix these?
faq.a: No. All five gaps are configuration and validation problems inside records Business Central already has: the item card, item references, item units of measure, the ship-to address, and the assembly BOM. The work is deciding which check runs before transmission and where it runs, not changing systems.

title: Smaller CPG Brands Fund a 68-Day Cash Gap. Two Free Tools Show Yours.
description: Brands under $10B carry a 68-day cash gap. The largest CPG companies carry none. Two free SEC-data tools measure yours.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard diagram of cash flowing from retailers to large CPG brands to smaller brands
answer: The median CPG company over $10B in revenue has a cash conversion cycle of about -3 days, so it collects before it pays suppliers. The median public CPG company under $10B carries a 68-day gap, per Pixels and Clicks analysis of SEC 10-K filings. Two free tools measure your own gap and customer concentration.
answerQualifier: Based on Pixels and Clicks analysis of 10-K filings from 19 retailers and 58 CPG manufacturers, October 2026.

faq.q: What is the cash conversion cycle for CPG companies?
faq.a: The cash conversion cycle is days to collect from customers, plus days of inventory, minus days payable. In 10-K filings analyzed by Pixels and Clicks, the median CPG company over $10B in revenue runs about -3 days. The median public CPG company under $10B runs 68 days. That company funds more than two months of its own working capital.

faq.q: Does Walmart owe its suppliers more than its inventory is worth?
faq.a: Yes, on its balance sheet. At the end of January 2026, Walmart reported $63.1B in accounts payable and $58.9B in inventory. Payables equaled 107% of inventory, up from 84% in January 2009. Accounts payable covers all of Walmart's vendors, not only CPG brands.

faq.q: How dependent are CPG companies on Walmart?
faq.a: Pixels and Clicks found 22 public CPG companies that reported Walmart's share of their sales in both 2009 and 2024. Of those, 14 now depend on Walmart more. Their median Walmart share rose from 18.5% to 22%. John B. Sanfilippo reported the largest rise, from 19% of net sales in fiscal 2009 to 41% in fiscal 2026.

faq.q: Is days payable the same as payment terms?
faq.a: No. Days payable is a balance-sheet ratio: accounts payable divided by cost of sales, times 365. It shows how long a company holds its bills on average. Payment terms are what a buyer and supplier agree in a contract. The two move together but are not the same number.

faq.q: Where can I download the data?
faq.a: Both datasets are free to download as CSV files from The Float and the Walmart Dependency Tracker on pixelsandclicks.net. Every figure links to the 10-K filing it comes from. You can use the charts and data in your own work with a link back.

faq.q: Can I download charts from the research pages?
faq.a: Yes. Every chart on The Float and the Walmart Dependency Tracker has a PNG download button. Hover over any chart figure to reveal it. The exported image is 2x resolution with a white background, ready for slides or reports.

faq.q: Can I link to a specific section of a research page?
faq.a: Yes. Hover over any section heading to reveal a # link. Click it to copy a direct URL to that section. The recipient lands on that heading.

faq.q: Can I share my Deduction Census benchmark results?
faq.a: Yes. After entering your numbers in the benchmark calculator, click 'Copy link to this result.' The URL encodes your deduction rate, disputed share, win rate, revenue, size band, and retailer. Anyone who opens that link sees the same comparison.

title: The Real Cost of Manual Data Entry at a Mid-Market CPG
description: Re-keying labor is the visible cost. Deductions, reconciliation hours, and rush freight stack on top. Free calculator inside.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: the visible labor cost of manual data entry versus the hidden cost in deductions, reconciliation, and freight
answer: The full annual cost of manual data entry between your WMS, EDI, and ERP is more than copy pasting from one system to another. It also includes deductions from bad ASNs, hours reconciling mismatched reports, and rush freight from stale data, plus margin loss and stockout risk no report captures. In the calculator's default scenario, those three quantifiable lines roughly double the labor-only estimate.
answerQualifier: Based on Pixels and Clicks' own manual data entry cost calculator methodology, cross-referenced with the deduction write-off pattern described in this site's EDI 856 coverage and the industry out-of-stock research cited in this site's OTIF coverage, August 2026.

faq.q: Why does the manual data entry cost calculator ask for deductions and freight costs, not just labor hours?
faq.a: Labor hours are the visible part of what manual data entry costs. The rest lands on other reports under other names: deductions traced to bad ASNs, hours spent reconciling reports that disagree, and rush freight caused by stale data. Adding those in gives the full annual cost, not just the part that shows up on a labor spreadsheet.

faq.q: Where do I find the 'data-error incidents per month' number the calculator asks for?
faq.a: Your EDI portal or retailer scorecard. Count last month's rejected 824s, ASN rejections, and manual order corrections across every retailer account you run, and use that total.

faq.q: Is the 2x multiplier in the calculator's example the same for every company?
faq.a: No. It's the ratio produced by the calculator's starting defaults: three coordinators, twenty incidents a month, four reconciliation hours a week. Enter your own five numbers and the ratio will move, higher for some operations, lower for others.

faq.q: What if I don't track reconciliation hours or expedite premiums yet?
faq.a: Estimate them for a first pass. A rough number beats leaving the field at zero, which understates the total. The standing meeting where two systems disagree and the rush charge on a recent freight invoice are both easy to reconstruct from memory even without a formal log.

faq.q: Does the calculator account for stockouts or lost shelf space?
faq.a: No, and that's on purpose. Stockout risk and buyer trust are real costs of manual data entry, but they're not consistent enough dollar figures to model in a calculator. The five inputs it does ask for are all costs you can pull from an existing report, which keeps the output defensible instead of speculative.

faq.q: How is this different from the OTIF calculator?
faq.a: The OTIF calculator prices a shipment-performance gap against retailer fine schedules. The manual data entry cost calculator prices the re-entry between your systems: labor, rework, deductions, reconciliation time, and rush freight. That's what often causes the gap in the first place.

title: The Deduction Dispute Windows at Walmart, Target, Amazon, Kroger
description: Dispute windows for Walmart, Target, Amazon, and Kroger deductions in one table, with the portal and channel to file through for each.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style reference table with four retailer columns labeled Walmart, Target, Amazon, and Kroger, each with a clock icon showing a different dispute deadline window, a stick figure holding a calendar with question marks, and a bold hand-lettered headline reading Dispute Deadlines
answer: Walmart gives up to two years to dispute most AP deductions through APDP, with shorter windows for chargebacks and shortages. Target allows 18 months prepaid and 9 months collect, through Synergy. Amazon chargebacks must be disputed within 30 days. Kroger gives 180 days through Supplier Connect, and reportedly 60 on an MCB fee.
answerQualifier: Compiled from six independent vendor sources (SPS Commerce/SupplierWiki, iNymbus, Glimpse, Confido, Adbrew, Consulterce), cross-referenced against each other, August 2026.

faq.q: How long do I have to dispute a Walmart deduction?
faq.a: It depends on the type. Up to two years for general AP deductions, 12 months for shortage claims, and 15 to 30 days for chargebacks, all through APDP per SPS Commerce and Glimpse. OTIF compliance chargebacks route through HighRadius instead, with a window closer to 30 days.

faq.q: What is Target's dispute deadline for shortages?
faq.a: Target's AP deduction window is 18 months from the document date on the check remittance for prepaid shipments. Collect shipments get 9 months from the shipping date, per SPS Commerce and iNymbus. Disputes go through Synergy, and a case returned as awaiting documentation auto-denies after 5 business days without a response.

faq.q: Can I dispute an Amazon chargeback more than once?
faq.a: Some chargeback types allow a second dispute after the first rejection, per Adbrew and Consulterce. The initial dispute must be filed within 30 days of the chargeback notification in Vendor Central. Sources differ on whether there is a hard cap on attempts.

faq.q: Where do I file a Kroger deduction dispute?
faq.a: You file through Supplier Connect, the PRGX-built platform that replaced the Lavante portal in late 2025, per iNymbus. The standard window is 180 days from the deduction date, per SPS Commerce and Confido. An MCB compliance fee is the exception, reportedly allowing 60 days and filing through the Kroger Supplier Hub instead. Once submitted, changes are not allowed, so documentation should be complete before filing.

faq.q: Do these deadlines ever change?
faq.a: Yes. Retailers update programs, rename portals, and adjust windows. This table was last reviewed in August 2026 and will be updated as sources report changes. If a deadline listed here does not match what you see in your own portal, let us know so we can correct it.

title: Deduction Management for CPG Suppliers: Stop the Leak at the Source
description: Deduction management is how CPG suppliers track, dispute, and prevent retail chargebacks. The codes, the dispute clock, and the root-cause fix that stops them from recurring.
author: Pixels and Clicks
pillarBlurb: The end-to-end system for tracking, disputing, and preventing retail deductions.
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard diagram of the deduction lifecycle: a coded remittance line decoded, validated, disputed with evidence, and the root cause fixed upstream
answer: Deduction management is the process a CPG supplier uses to track, validate, dispute, and prevent the chargebacks and shortages retailers pull off their payments. It covers decoding each remittance line, gathering shipment evidence, filing disputes before the deadline, and fixing the root cause in the ERP or EDI setup so the same deduction stops recurring.
answerQualifier: Based on retailer deduction and dispute processes documented across this site's Walmart, Target, Amazon, and Kroger coverage, November 2026. Programs and dispute windows change; confirm current terms in your own vendor portal.

faq.q: What is deduction management?
faq.a: Deduction management is how a supplier handles the chargebacks, shortages, and compliance fines a retailer deducts from its payments. It runs across four stages: decode the coded remittance line, validate whether the charge is real, dispute the invalid ones with evidence before the deadline, and fix the root cause so the deduction does not recur. Done well, it is a prevention discipline, not just a recovery chase.

faq.q: What are chargebacks in retail?
faq.a: A retail chargeback is a deduction a retailer takes off a supplier's payment for a shipment or document that broke a rule: a late delivery, a short count, a bad label, or a mismatched EDI file. It posts as a coded line on the remittance weeks after delivery and is separate from a product return. Each retailer uses its own code set and dispute portal.

faq.q: Is deduction management software or a service better?
faq.a: Software automates tracking and dispute filing, which helps at high volume, but most tools stop at recovery: chasing deductions after they post. For a mid-market CPG supplier the larger win is root cause, closing the ERP and EDI gaps that generate the charge in the first place. That is a service and process question, not only a software one, so the two are complements rather than substitutes.

faq.q: How do you reduce retail deductions?
faq.a: Start by separating the pattern from the noise: which code, at which retailer, from which cause. Validate before you pay, because a share of deductions are duplicates or invalid. Dispute the recoverable ones inside the window. Then fix the upstream data or document gap, since many deductions trace to an ASN, invoice, or unit-of-measure mismatch rather than a warehouse failure.

faq.q: How long do you have to dispute a deduction?
faq.a: The clock is set per retailer and it is unforgiving. Walmart disputes run through APDP in Retail Link, Amazon through Vendor Central, and Target and Kroger through their own portals, each with a different window. Miss the deadline and a preventable, disputable charge becomes permanent, so the dispute clock usually matters more than the merits of the case.

title: Is Your Data Ready for Netstock, o9, or Blue Yonder?
description: The six data-readiness checks that decide whether a Netstock, o9, or Blue Yonder pilot ships a working forecast at your SKU catalog.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: what demand forecasting for CPG requires
answer: CPG demand-forecasting data readiness means your SKU history, unit-of-measure consistency, promotional flagging, and master-data hygiene can support a statistical model before you buy one. A platform can run a technically correct forecast on messy inputs and still produce numbers you shouldn't order against. The six checks: history depth, UOM consistency, promo/baseline separation, master-data change control, stockout-vs-zero-demand distinction, and accuracy tracking.
answerQualifier: Based on Oracle NetSuite's demand-planning documentation, the Institute of Business Forecasting's MAPE reference, and CPG-specific trade-promotion forecasting guidance (Vividly), August 2026.

faq.q: How many years of sales history does a demand-forecasting platform need?
faq.a: There's no universal number, and Oracle's own NetSuite demand-planning documentation doesn't state a minimum. What matters is continuity: enough clean periods to separate a real trend or seasonal pattern from ordinary noise. A seasonal category typically needs at least two full cycles to tell the two apart. Less than a year, or a year full of gaps, is the tier our own readiness quiz scores as not ready.

faq.q: What is MAPE, and what counts as a good score?
faq.a: MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error) averages the absolute percentage gap between what you forecast and what actually sold. There's no universal "good" threshold; it depends on category, volatility, and horizon length. What matters more than the number itself is whether you're tracking it consistently enough to know if it's improving.

faq.q: Can I run a forecasting platform if my promotional and base demand aren't separated yet?
faq.a: You can run it, but expect the forecast to be wrong in a predictable direction. A quarter with a major promotion inflates what the model treats as your steady-state baseline, so the next quarter's forecast inherits demand that isn't there, and you over-buy against it. Separate the two before go-live if you can; if you can't, treat the first two quarters of forecasts as suspect.

faq.q: What's the difference between a stockout and real zero demand in forecasting data?
faq.a: A stockout is demand that existed and went unmet; a zero-demand period is demand that genuinely wasn't there. Sales history records both as the same zero. A model that can't tell them apart learns that an item sells less than it does, and forecasts accordingly, training itself cycle after cycle to keep you understocked on exactly the items that stocked out before.

title: EDI 810: How One Pack-Size Field Becomes a Shortage Deduction
description: One pack-size mismatch in your item file, carried through the 850, 856, and 810, becomes a shortage deduction for goods that actually arrived.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: EDI 810 invoice document chain: 850 to 856 to 810 three-way match producing a shortage deduction
answer: The retailer's AP department compares three records before releasing payment: the 850 purchase order, the receiving scan (staged by the 856 ASN), and the 810 invoice. When the quantities across those three disagree, the system records a shortage, not a data error. Most shortage deductions trace to a stale item-file field, a wrong unit of measure or an outdated case-pack count, that traveled through every document unchallenged until the receiving scan disagreed with the invoice.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 810 transaction-set structure (Stedi, BOLD VAN, Celigo, SignalEDI documentation), SPS Commerce shortage-cause references, and Microsoft Learn three-way-match documentation, August 2026. Segment names are the public standard; individual retailer tolerance rules and match thresholds vary.

faq.q: What is an EDI 810?
faq.a: The EDI 810 is the electronic invoice a supplier transmits after shipping. It carries the invoice number, PO reference, line-item quantities, unit prices, and the total amount due. The retailer's AP department compares it against the original purchase order (850) and the advance ship notice (856) before releasing payment.

faq.q: Why did I get a shortage deduction when everything shipped?
faq.a: The retailer's three-way match compares what you invoiced against what their receiving scan recorded, not against what physically arrived. If your 810 bills 120 eaches and their system expected 10 cases of 12, the match fails even though the same goods are on the dock. The mismatch is in the data, not the warehouse.

faq.q: What is a three-way match in retail AP?
faq.a: A three-way match compares three records before paying an invoice: the purchase order (what was ordered), the receiving record (what the warehouse counted, staged by the ASN), and the invoice (what the supplier billed). Any disagreement among the three becomes a short-pay or a deduction code on the remittance.

faq.q: What's the difference between an 810 and an 856?
faq.a: The 856 Advance Ship Notice describes what's in a shipment before or as it moves. The 810 invoice bills for it afterward. They should describe the same quantities, and when they don't, that gap is where most shortage-code deductions originate. For the full 856 breakdown, see [EDI 856 (ASN): why retailers reject it](/articles/edi-856-asn-rejections.html).

faq.q: Can I dispute an invoice-adjustment deduction?
faq.a: Usually yes, if you have the evidence: a signed bill of lading or proof of delivery showing the correct quantity, the original PO, and the ASN. The dispute window varies by retailer. See the [dispute-deadline reference table](/articles/deduction-dispute-deadlines-by-retailer.html) for reported timelines.

title: EDI 824: How to Read the Rejection Codes
description: The EDI 824 tells you why a transmission failed, not just whether it arrived. How OTI and TED segments work, and why an unresolved 824 becomes a deduction.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram explaining the EDI 824 Application Advice: a document flowing through an OTI segment check and a TED error-code segment, labeled with arrows, showing how an unresolved rejection turns into a deduction weeks later
answer: The EDI 824 Application Advice tells a trading partner why a document's content, not its syntax, failed: a duplicate invoice, an out-of-balance total, a missing reference. It arrives after a clean 997 confirms only that the transmission was structurally valid. An unresolved 824 rejection routinely becomes a deduction on the remittance weeks later, with nothing connecting the two.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 824 transaction-set structure (Stedi's EDI reference), Kroger's public EDI portal error-code documentation, and LearnEDI.org's 824 reference, August 2026. Segment names and the OTI/TED structure are the public standard; individual retailers layer their own longer error-code catalogs on top.

faq.q: What's the difference between a 997 and an 824?
faq.a: The 997 Functional Acknowledgment confirms a transmission arrived and parsed as valid EDI syntax, nothing about whether the business content makes sense. The 824 Application Advice is what tells you the content itself was rejected or flagged: a duplicate invoice, a total that doesn't balance, a reference the retailer's system doesn't recognize. For the full side-by-side comparison, see [EDI 997 vs. 824](https://www.pixelsandclicks.net/articles/edi-997-vs-824.html).

faq.q: Is an 824 rejection the same as a chargeback?
faq.a: Not directly. The 824 is a data-validation response, not a deduction. But an 824 you don't act on routinely becomes one. If the underlying document (an invoice or ASN) never gets corrected and resent, the mismatch it flagged shows up as a shortage or pricing deduction on a later remittance.

faq.q: Do all retailers send 824s?
faq.a: No. Some retailers validate content and simply deduct silently if something doesn't match, with no 824 program at all. Where an 824 program exists, it's the closest thing to a free early-warning system a supplier gets before a deduction shows up.

faq.q: What does TED01 mean on an 824?
faq.a: TED01 is the numeric error condition code inside the Technical Error Description segment. It's a small, generic list, things like 006 (Duplicate) or 007 (Missing Data). Read it together with TED02, the free-text field where the retailer explains what specifically triggered it.

title: EDI 856 (ASN): Why Retailers Reject It
description: What the EDI 856 Advance Ship Notice carries, the six most common reasons retailers reject it, and which deduction it becomes if you don't catch it.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram explaining the EDI 856 Advance Ship Notice: a truck and a shipment carton labeled with carton counts, SSCC labels, and item quantities, with an arrow showing a rejected ASN turning into a shortage deduction
answer: The EDI 856 Advance Ship Notice tells a retailer what's in a shipment before it physically arrives: carton counts, SSCC labels, and item quantities in a hierarchical structure. When it's late, mismatched, or structurally wrong, the retailer's system doesn't record a data error. It records a shortage or a chargeback that shows up weeks later on a remittance.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 856 transaction-set structure (Stedi's EDI reference, SupplyPike/SPS Commerce documentation), August 2026. Segment names and hierarchy are the public standard; individual retailer implementation guides vary in which segments are required.

faq.q: What happens if an 856 is rejected?
faq.a: Depends on the retailer's system. Some reject the transmission outright and send back a 997 or 824 flagging the error, which you can fix and resend before the truck arrives. But a clean 997 by itself only confirms the file parsed, not that the content was accepted (see [EDI 997 vs. 824](https://www.pixelsandclicks.net/articles/edi-997-vs-824.html)). Others accept a structurally valid but inaccurate 856, and the mismatch surfaces later as a receiving discrepancy: no error message, just a deduction weeks after the fact.

faq.q: How late can an ASN be before it counts against you?
faq.a: There's no single standard window. Each retailer sets its own. Most require transmission before the shipment physically arrives, not before it leaves your dock.

faq.q: Does a rejected 856 always mean a deduction?
faq.a: No, but it removes your best evidence. The ASN is the record of what you say you shipped. Without it, you're arguing a shortage or pricing dispute with no proof on your side.

faq.q: What's the difference between an 856 and an 810?
faq.a: The 856 is the Advance Ship Notice, sent before or as the shipment moves. The [810 is the invoice](/articles/edi-810-invoice-mismatch-deductions.html), generated afterward to bill for it. They should describe the same quantities, and when they don't, that gap is where most shortage-code deductions originate.

title: EDI 997 vs. 824: What Flags a Failure
description: A clean 997 only confirms your EDI transmission parsed, not that the retailer accepted the content. What each acknowledgment actually checks.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram comparing the EDI 997 Functional Acknowledgment and 824 Application Advice: a document passing a syntax check labeled 997, then a content check labeled 824, with a branch showing what happens when no 824 exists
answer: The EDI 997 Functional Acknowledgment confirms only that a transmission parsed as valid syntax, not that the retailer accepted the content. The EDI 824 Application Advice reports that separately, later, and only where a retailer chooses to send one. A clean 997 with no follow-up 824 is not proof of acceptance.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 997 and 824 transaction-set structure (Stedi's EDI reference), Kroger's public EDI portal documentation, and LearnEDI.org's acknowledgment references, August 2026. Segment names and the two-document structure are the public standard; which retailers run an 824 program at all is implementation-specific and not universal.

faq.q: What's the difference between a 997 and an 824?
faq.a: The 997 Functional Acknowledgment confirms a transmission arrived and parsed as valid EDI syntax, nothing about the business content. The 824 Application Advice reports whether that content was actually accepted, once the retailer's system tries to process it. That content might be an invoice total, a PO reference, or a shipment quantity. They answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.

faq.q: If I get a clean 997, does that mean my EDI document was accepted?
faq.a: No. It means the envelope was structurally valid, right segments, right order, right delimiters. Whether the retailer's system did anything useful with the content inside is a separate question. Where an 824 exists, it answers that question later. Where it doesn't, the question goes unanswered.

faq.q: Do all retailers send an 824?
faq.a: No. Some retailers validate content and simply deduct against the remittance if something doesn't match, with no application-advice program at all. Where that's the case, a clean 997 is the only acknowledgment you'll ever get, and it was never designed to tell you what you're using it for.

faq.q: Is a rejected 824 the same as a chargeback?
faq.a: Not directly. It's a data-validation response, not a deduction. But an 824 rejection that goes uncorrected routinely becomes one. The gap between the two is usually 30 or more days, with nothing on the remittance connecting the eventual deduction back to the written warning that preceded it.

faq.q: What should I actually monitor if I only get 997s?
faq.a: Watch the receiving and payment signals downstream of the document itself, since there's no earlier warning coming. That means tracking invoice-to-payment variance, unexpected remittance deduction codes, and receiving discrepancies as the de facto acknowledgment, weeks later than an 824 would have told you.

title: Why Your ERP Says Shipped and the Retailer Says Short
description: Four quantities from four systems create one shortage deduction. Trace from PO to ERP to WMS to ASN to receipt, find the first mismatch, and stop guessing.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Four quantities from four systems creating one shortage deduction: PO, ERP, WMS, and retailer receipt diverging into a gap
answer: A shortage deduction usually comes from a mismatch between four numbers: ordered quantity (from the PO), picked quantity (from the WMS), ASN quantity (from the EDI 856), and received quantity (from the retailer portal). Your ERP may show shipped because the shipment was posted. That doesn't prove the retailer received the same units, cases, or cartons. It also doesn't prove the ASN matched the physical shipment. To fix the deduction, trace one SKU through the full chain and find the first place the numbers diverge.
answerQualifier: Based on public documentation from Oracle NetSuite (item fulfillment, units of measure), Microsoft Learn (Business Central item references, warehouse posting, units of measure), SPS Commerce (EDI chargebacks), BOLD VAN (EDI mapping failures), Endless Commerce (shortage deduction benchmarks), and Confido (deduction recovery), September 2026. Individual ERP configurations and retailer receiving rules vary.

faq.q: Why does my ERP say shipped when the retailer deducted for shortage?
faq.a: A posted shipment means the ERP transaction moved forward. It doesn't prove the truck carried that exact quantity. The gap usually comes from one of four places: a pick exception posted after order release, a 3PL edit made in a portal your ERP doesn't see, a unit-of-measure mismatch between your system and the retailer's, or an ASN that transmitted a different quantity than the physical shipment.

faq.q: Can a unit-of-measure mismatch cause a shortage deduction even when nothing is physically missing?
faq.a: Yes. If your ASN declares 120 eaches and the retailer's system expected 10 cases of 12, the quantities are mathematically identical but the formats don't reconcile. The receiving count reads short. The retailer files a shortage deduction for goods that physically arrived. The fix is in your item master, not on the truck.

faq.q: How do I find the root cause of a shortage deduction?
faq.a: Pick one deducted PO and trace one SKU. Pull the retailer PO, ERP sales order, pick ticket, ASN file, 997 and 824 responses, BOL, POD, retailer receiving record, invoice, and remittance line. Put the quantities in one row. The first place they diverge is your root cause.

faq.q: Does a NetSuite or Business Central shipment posting prove in-full delivery?
faq.a: No. A posted shipment confirms the ERP transaction completed. It doesn't confirm the warehouse picked that exact quantity, the ASN transmitted the same number, or the retailer received it. The gap between the ERP posting and the retailer's receiving record is where most shortage deductions originate.

title: The Retailer's Peak Forecast Will Cost You OTIF in November
description: Peak-season retailer forecasts overstate demand. Accepting one without a counter-model stacks OTIF risk in November and inventory write-downs in January.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Whiteboard-style diagram of a CPG supplier receiving an inflated Q4 forecast from a retailer, showing the branching risks of accepting it uncritically: OTIF fine in November, shortage claims in December, and markdown deductions in January
answer: Retailer peak-season forecasts routinely overstate demand by 10 to 25 percent, and accepting one without running a supplier-side counter-forecast commits you to inventory and capacity you may not clear. The trap is not the forecast. The trap is treating it as an order commitment. Build a POS-driven counter-forecast, flag any line where the retailer number sits more than 15 percent above your own, and negotiate the delta before you cut a purchase order to your co-packer.
answerQualifier: Based on public forecasting and retailer-compliance documentation from SPS Commerce, BOLD VAN, Endless Commerce, and Supply Chain Dive, September 2026. Retailer forecast tools and thresholds vary by program.

faq.q: Why do retailer peak-season forecasts overstate demand?
faq.a: Category buyers face asymmetric risk. An out-of-stock at peak costs them shelf space and a sales miss. An overstock at peak costs them a markdown that hits the supplier through code 10 or a return. The rational buyer forecast leans high because the downside falls on your P&L, not theirs. This shows up most in first-year holiday programs and in categories with new SKU launches.

faq.q: What should I do when a retailer forecast is 20% above my POS trend?
faq.a: Send a counter-forecast referencing your own POS data, last year's sell-through at the same account, and any current velocity signal. Ask the buyer for the assumption behind the peak lift. Do not decline. Propose a stepped commitment: firm on the first half, flexible on the second, with a case-pack contingency plan. Buyers negotiate this every year. Suppliers who accept without pushing back carry the write-down alone.

faq.q: How does an inflated peak forecast create OTIF risk?
faq.a: Two paths. The first: you commit inventory, freight, and DC space to the inflated line, then a mid-November PO cut leaves the balance stranded. Your OTIF drops on the next PO because you rerouted capacity to hit the peak plan. The second: the retailer holds the forecast, sell-through underperforms, and the retailer marks down or returns the excess in January. That comes back as code 10 or codes 92, 93, 94.

faq.q: Can I dispute an OTIF fine caused by a retailer forecast miss?
faq.a: The OTIF fine is a program-level chargeback measured on your aggregate on-time and in-full rate, not a per-shipment dispute. A forecast miss that damaged your fill rate is not disputable as an OTIF line. You can dispute the underlying shortage codes on the specific POs, but not the scorecard math. The prevention is upstream, before the forecast becomes an order.

faq.q: What is the cost of accepting a peak forecast without a counter-model?
faq.a: It varies with category and lift, but a typical outcome for a $50 million CPG supplier accepting a 20 percent inflated Q4 forecast: two to three points of OTIF drop in November, 60 to 90 days of unproductive inventory carrying cost, and a January markdown deduction of 1 to 3 percent of the affected receipts. The forecast decision in September is a working-capital decision as much as a fill-rate decision.

title: The Home Depot Routing Guide Rules That Cost Suppliers Most

answer: Home Depot's routing guide requires suppliers to book collect shipments through its assigned carriers and TMS, hit a reported 90% on-time threshold, transmit an EDI 856 ASN before the shipment reaches the DC, and label cartons to GS1-128 spec. Violations, including using the wrong carrier on an on-time shipment, post as chargebacks deducted from the next payment.
answerQualifier: Compiled from public freight, EDI, and logistics vendor documentation (DTS One, WarehouseQuote, Productiv, SPS Commerce, Crstl, Foundational, plus one vendor blog, iNymbus, flagged inline), August 2026. No figure confirmed against Home Depot's own Supplier Hub.

faq.q: What is Home Depot's routing guide?
faq.a: It's the document and TMS ruleset, published through Home Depot's Supplier Self-Service portal, that assigns which carrier a supplier must use for a given collect shipment based on the ship method listed on the PO. It covers shipments into the continental US, Canada, and Puerto Rico, per DTS One.

faq.q: How much is a Home Depot routing guide violation?
faq.a: DTS One reports a $250 penalty for using a carrier other than the one Home Depot's routing guide assigns, applied even when the shipment itself arrives on time. No second public source confirms this exact figure, so treat it as reported, not verified.

faq.q: Do I have to use Home Depot's assigned carrier even if my own carrier is cheaper or faster?
