title: How to Dispute a Walmart Deduction: APDP, HighRadius, and the Timer That Closes Cases Early
description: Step-by-step guide to disputing Walmart deductions through APDP and HighRadius, with documentation requirements and the 14-day draft timer that closes valid claims before the posted deadline.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn black ink whiteboard with HOW TO DISPUTE WALMART DEDUCTIONS in bold uppercase at the top, a flowchart splitting a remittance notice into two paths — APDP inside Retail Link for AP deductions and HighRadius for OTIF chargebacks — with a clock labeled 14-DAY DRAFT TIMER and a documentation stack labeled SIGNED POD, BOL, INVOICE
answer: Walmart AP deductions and shortage claims dispute through APDP inside Retail Link. OTIF compliance chargebacks go to HighRadius — a separate system outside Retail Link. APDP has a 14-day internal draft timer: a case you open but don't submit within 14 days auto-closes without warning. The posted windows are 2 years for general AP deductions, 12 months for shortage claims, and 15 to 30 days for compliance chargebacks. Filing in the wrong portal, or leaving a case as a draft, is how valid disputes expire before the posted deadline.
answerQualifier: Portal and window data from SPS Commerce, Glimpse, and Confido, cross-referenced August 2026. Walmart adjusts programs through Retail Link without public announcements; confirm windows in your own portal before filing.

faq.q: What is APDP and where do I find it?
faq.a: APDP stands for Accounts Payable Deduction Portal. It's Walmart's primary dispute filing system, accessible from inside Retail Link. Most deduction types — AP deductions, shortage claims, billing errors, routing chargebacks — route through APDP. OTIF compliance chargebacks are the exception and go to HighRadius instead.

faq.q: How do I know if a Walmart deduction goes to APDP or HighRadius?
faq.a: OTIF compliance chargebacks route to HighRadius. All other deduction types — shortages, AP deductions, invoice errors, routing chargebacks — go to APDP. Filing an OTIF chargeback in APDP results in rejection without review. The HighRadius window is 30 days from the chargeback notice. Use the Deduction Code Decoder to confirm which portal your code uses before you open a case.

faq.q: What is the 14-day draft timer in APDP?
faq.a: When you open a dispute case in APDP, it saves as a draft. If you don't submit the draft within 14 days, the case auto-closes. APDP doesn't send a warning before it closes. The draft timer runs from when you first open the case, not from when you attach documents or think you've hit submit. This timer is separate from the posted dispute window and can expire a valid claim weeks before the published deadline.

faq.q: What documentation does Walmart require for a shortage claim?
faq.a: At minimum: a signed proof of delivery, bill of lading, carrier confirmation of delivery, and the original invoice. For a quantity shortage, packing slips showing what physically shipped also help. Walmart can deny a shortage dispute if the POD isn't signed by a receiver at the DC. Gather the full package before you open the case in APDP — the 14-day draft timer starts the moment you open it.

faq.q: How long does it take Walmart to resolve a dispute?
faq.a: AP deduction disputes through APDP take 60 to 90 days on average. Shortage claims run longer if Walmart opens an internal receiving investigation. HighRadius OTIF disputes typically resolve faster but within the tight 30-day window. APDP shows status codes — Pending, Under Review, Additional Documentation Requested — but doesn't estimate a resolution date.

faq.q: Can I reopen a closed APDP dispute?
faq.a: No. A case that closes — either because the 14-day draft timer expired or because Walmart denied it — can't be reopened through APDP. Some suppliers escalate through their Walmart buyer or category manager. The cleaner path is submitting complete documentation before the internal timer expires.

title: Kroger Deduction Codes 2-9 and the 180-Day Dispute Clock
description: Kroger deduction codes 2 through 9, the ORAD and MCB compliance fees, and the Supplier Connect dispute path. 180 days to file, 60 on MCB.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram showing a Kroger remittance line with a numeric deduction code circled, an arrow pointing to a stack of vendor-source PDFs labeled SPS Commerce, iNymbus, and Confido, and a second arrow pointing to a portal window labeled Supplier Connect (formerly Lavante), with a stick figure holding a magnifying glass and a bold hand-lettered headline reading Kroger Deductions
answer: Kroger bills suppliers on two tracks. AP codes 2 through 9 cover shortages, cost differences, and promotional allowances, with 180 days to dispute. Compliance fees like ORAD and MCB post as AR deductions instead, and an MCB fee reportedly allows only 60 days. Disputes file through Supplier Connect, which replaced Lavante in late 2025.
answerQualifier: Compiled from six independent public vendor sources (SPS Commerce, iNymbus, Confido, WarehouseQuote, ClearChain, SupplierWiki/SupplyPike), August 2026. Kroger does not publish this itself, so every figure here is vendor-reported and flagged where sources disagree. Confirm the code and window on your own Supplier Connect remittance detail.

faq.q: What deduction codes does Kroger use on a remittance?
faq.a: Vendor sources describe eight primary AP codes (2 through 9) covering promotional allowance differences, cost mismatches, shortages, EDI non-compliance, unit shortages, overages, net-dollar catch-alls, and pickup allowances. Letter codes like SH (shortage), LC (list cost), and SD (shorted deals) appear alongside the numeric list. Compliance fees like ORAD (late delivery) and MCB (merchandising) post separately as AR deductions, not AP.

faq.q: How long do I have to dispute a Kroger deduction?
faq.a: 180 days from the deduction date for standard AP deductions, per SPS Commerce and Confido. An MCB compliance fee reportedly allows only 60 days from the MCB issue date and files through the Kroger Supplier Hub instead, per ClearChain. Once a claim is submitted it cannot be modified, so documentation has to be complete before filing.

faq.q: What is the difference between Lavante and Supplier Connect?
faq.a: Lavante was Kroger's previous PRGX-hosted dispute portal. Supplier Connect is the replacement Kroger rolled out in late 2025 with the same operator, migrated historical data, and Partner Pass single sign-on, per iNymbus. The 180-day window and PRGX review did not change. Guidance published before mid-2026 still names Lavante, so treat it as stale on portal mechanics.

faq.q: What is a Kroger ORAD fine?
faq.a: ORAD stands for Original Requested Arrival Date, the delivery date on your Kroger PO. Miss it and Kroger applies a late-shipment fine. Per iNymbus, ORAD is tracked against a 98% on-time threshold with a 95% case fill rate on every shipment. ORAD fines post as AR deductions on a different claim path than the numeric AP codes, per SPS Commerce.

faq.q: How does Kroger's deduction program compare to Walmart's?
faq.a: Walmart runs roughly 90 AP codes, disputes through APDP, and allows up to two years on general deductions. Kroger runs eight numeric codes plus letter codes, disputes through Supplier Connect, and allows 180 days. Kroger also splits compliance fees onto a separate AR track, whereas Walmart deducts everything through the same AP flow.

title: The 30-Minute Deduction Triage Before Your OTIF Meeting
description: Nine checks before the weekly OTIF meeting, four timestamps that replace carrier blame, and a script that turns scorecard panic into one next action per PO.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: OTIF deduction triage checklist with nine checks before the Monday scorecard meeting
answer: Before blaming the carrier for an OTIF deduction, check nine things in order: PO version match, pick completion, ASN-to-pick match, ASN send time against the retailer cutoff, 997 acknowledgment, 824 content response, appointment request timing, carrier arrival time, and retailer receiving record. The first mismatch you find is your root cause. Pull four timestamps for each flagged PO before the meeting starts: pick confirm, ASN send, appointment confirmation, and retailer receipt.
answerQualifier: Based on public EDI and compliance documentation from SPS Commerce, BOLD VAN, Confido, Endless Commerce, and DOSS, September 2026. Individual retailer scoring rules, dispute windows, and chargeback thresholds vary by program.

faq.q: What should I check before blaming the carrier for an OTIF deduction?
faq.a: Check nine things: whether the PO changed after confirmation, whether the warehouse picked the full quantity, whether the ASN matched the pick, whether the ASN transmitted before the retailer's cutoff, whether the 997 came back clean, whether an 824 flagged a content error, whether the delivery appointment was requested on time, whether the carrier arrived inside the window, and whether the retailer's receiving record matched the ASN. The first mismatch tells you where to work.

faq.q: How do I run a 30-minute OTIF deduction meeting?
faq.a: Use this order: Finance shows the deduction line and dollar amount. Ops pulls the affected POs. Warehouse shows pick completion and short-pick exceptions. The EDI owner shows ASN send time, 997, and 824 status. Logistics shows the appointment and delivery trail. Then tag each PO as dispute, fix, carrier, or unknown, and assign one next action per PO.

faq.q: What four timestamps should I pull before an OTIF meeting?
faq.a: Pick confirm time (when the warehouse finished the order), ASN send time (when the retailer was told what was coming), appointment confirmation time (whether the delivery slot was real), and arrival or receipt time (whether freight hit the window). If those four don't line up, you don't have a freight issue yet. You have a timeline issue.

faq.q: Can a clean 997 mean my ASN still failed?
faq.a: Yes. A 997 confirms the file parsed without syntax errors. It doesn't confirm the retailer accepted the business content: quantities, item identifiers, pack hierarchy, or shipment date. Business-level rejection comes back on the 824, if the retailer sends one. A clean 997 with no 824 follow-up is not proof of acceptance.

title: The Five NetSuite Settings Behind Your ASN Rejections
description: Five NetSuite-specific reasons the EDI 856 ASN comes out wrong: item cross-references, UOM conversion, pick timing, subsidiary mapping, kit explosion.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: NetSuite's EDI 856 document failure
answer: A NetSuite-generated EDI 856 that's wrong at transmission becomes a shortage or no-merchandise deduction thirty to sixty days later. Five NetSuite-specific gaps cause it: item cross-references, eaches-to-cases unit conversion, pick-confirm timing, OneWorld subsidiary routing, and kit or assembly explosion into pack-level detail. Each is catchable pre-transmission with a saved search or SuiteFlow validation.
answerQualifier: Based on Oracle NetSuite's own help documentation (item records, units of measure, item fulfillment, OneWorld) and EDI-connector vendor documentation (Orderful, Celigo), August 2026. NetSuite's native fields and statuses are documented. Which specific validations a given connector runs pre-transmission varies by vendor and is not a public standard.

faq.q: Does NetSuite generate the EDI 856 natively, or does it need a connector?
faq.a: NetSuite's Item Fulfillment record holds most of the data an 856 needs, but NetSuite does not natively speak X12. An EDI connector (Orderful, Celigo, SPS Commerce, TrueCommerce, and others) reads the fulfillment record and maps it into the transaction set. Several connectors add custom fields to capture pallet/carton detail that Item Fulfillment does not represent on its own.

faq.q: Can a unit-of-measure mismatch cause a shortage deduction even when the physical count was correct?
faq.a: Yes. If the 856 declares a quantity in eaches where the retailer's implementation guide expects cases, the receiving count looks short or over by exactly the case-pack multiplier. Nothing is physically wrong. It reads as a shortage code on the remittance regardless.

faq.q: Why does a kit or assembly item break an 856 that a simple inventory item doesn't?
faq.a: A retailer's system expects pack-level detail: which item, in what quantity, in which carton. A kit item is one line in NetSuite but multiple physical components on the truck. As a result, the 856 has to explode the kit into its components at the pack level. That explosion logic lives in the connector, not in NetSuite's native fulfillment screen.

faq.q: Does a NetSuite OneWorld subsidiary structure affect EDI routing?
faq.a: It can. Each OneWorld transaction generally posts to one subsidiary, and each subsidiary has its own locations. If a trading-partner or ship-to mapping points to the wrong subsidiary's location, the fulfillment record can carry the wrong facility or tax jurisdiction into the outbound 856. That's an error a receiving DC has no way to catch on its end.

faq.q: What's the fastest way to start catching these before they become deductions?
faq.a: Pick the one failure mode you have already seen on a remittance and build a saved search for it first: unmapped vendor item codes, fulfillments missing a UOM conversion, or kit lines with no component detail. A single working validation beats a five-point plan that never ships.

title: What Changes in the Routing Guide From October to December
description: What tightens in retailer routing guides from October through December: MABD tolerance, appointment cutoffs, and ASN timing shifts, retailer by retailer.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Whiteboard-style matrix comparing peak-season routing guide changes across Walmart, Target, Home Depot, and Kroger, with columns for MABD tolerance, appointment cutoff, ASN cutoff, and receiving behavior
answer: The core routing rules do not always change for peak season, but the tolerance around them almost always does. Walmart holds the Must Arrive By Date window through peak but runs it against higher volume, so misses compound. Target compresses appointment windows in the last two weeks of November and December at high-volume DCs. Home Depot publishes peak-period addenda through its Vendor Compliance program. Kroger tightens receiving appointment cadence at high-volume DCs during peak. The pattern across all four is that measurement rules stay the same, and enforcement gets stricter.
answerQualifier: Based on public routing guide and vendor compliance documentation from Walmart, Target, Home Depot, Kroger, and industry vendor sources including SPS Commerce, SupplyPike, Confido, and Supply Chain Dive, September 2026. Retailer routing guides are updated by supplier portal notice and are not always publicly documented in full. Confirm current specifics in the relevant retailer portal before acting.

faq.q: What is a retailer routing guide, and why does it change for peak season?
faq.a: A retailer routing guide is the retailer's rulebook for how freight arrives at its DCs: MABD dates, appointment procedures, carrier selection, load consolidation, and ASN cutoffs. The rules themselves rarely change for peak. What changes is the tolerance: fewer late-appointment overrides, tighter enforcement of load-consolidation rules, faster dock rejections when paperwork is off. Peak is when the routing guide gets enforced to the letter, not when the letter gets rewritten.

faq.q: Does Walmart change MABD tolerance in November and December?
faq.a: Walmart's MABD window and OTIF measurement thresholds have been publicly reported through the Retail Link portal rather than external press. Public reporting suggests Walmart holds the 90 percent on-time and 95 percent in-full targets for prepaid suppliers across the year, but the aggregate volume denominator during peak means small absolute misses cost more OTIF points than the same misses in June. Suppliers who track the fine dollar exposure rather than the percentage often see a threefold peak-to-mid-year variance without any rule change.

faq.q: How much lead time does Target require for peak appointments?
faq.a: Target's OTIF program uses MABD-based on-time measurement and appointment procedures documented in its vendor portal. Public vendor coverage indicates Target compresses appointment windows at high-volume DCs during peak, particularly in the two weeks leading up to Thanksgiving and Christmas. Specific cutoff hours are not publicly documented in full and vary by DC. Confirm the current Target Vendor Standards Manual and any peak addenda through Target Partners Online before shipping.

faq.q: What does Home Depot publish about peak-period routing?
faq.a: Home Depot maintains a Vendor Compliance program with a Supplier Expectation Rating (SER) and disputes route through Vendor Compliance Support. Home Depot publishes peak-period addenda to its supplier community through Vendor Standards updates. Public vendor coverage suggests these addenda cover appointment window compression at high-volume DCs from October through December, plus stricter enforcement of load-tender response times. Full addendum contents are not publicly documented; check Home Depot's supplier portal for current specifics.

faq.q: Does Kroger tighten routing rules for peak?
faq.a: Kroger operates supplier compliance through its supplier hub and Sync platform, with deduction and chargeback programs tied to shipment execution against the PO and MABD. Kroger runs a large peak grocery period around Thanksgiving and Christmas, and public vendor coverage indicates receiving appointment cadence tightens at high-volume DCs during that window. Kroger does not publish peak-specific addenda as broadly as some other retailers; the current shipment and routing rules are documented in the Kroger Supplier Hub.

title: The Q4 Deduction Cliff: A Month-by-Month Calendar
description: Retailer deductions do not spike evenly across Q4. OTIF fines hit in November, shortages pile up in December, the returns wave crests in January. The calendar.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Whiteboard-style calendar diagram of the Q4 deduction cliff for CPG suppliers, showing OTIF fines peaking in November, shortage claims peaking in December, and returns and markdown deductions peaking in January and February
answer: The Q4 deduction cliff runs October through February and hits three separate waves. OTIF fines and ASN failures peak in November when volume is highest against the tightest routing windows. Shortage and receiving claims peak in December when DC receiving speeds up and error rates rise. Markdown deductions under code 10 and returns under codes 92, 93, and 94 peak in January and February, after post-holiday sell-through gets counted. A supplier that plans against one flat Q4 chargeback rate underestimates the risk in each specific window.
answerQualifier: Based on public deduction and OTIF documentation from BOLD VAN, Endless Commerce, SPS Commerce, SupplyPike, and Supply Chain Dive, September 2026. Retailer deduction volumes and program details vary by account and year.

faq.q: Which deduction types actually spike in Q4?
faq.a: Three families spike, at different times. OTIF fines and ASN-related chargebacks peak in November because peak volume runs against tighter routing windows. Shortage and receiving deductions like Walmart code 22 and Target SIFR peak in December because DC receiving throughput rises and error rates rise with it. Markdown deductions like Walmart code 10 and returns under codes 92, 93, and 94 peak in January and February, when the retailer counts through post-holiday sell-through and returns.

faq.q: When does the peak-season OTIF fine window end?
faq.a: The measurement window and the payment window are different. The measurement window at Walmart, Target, and Kroger typically covers the receiving month, so a November miss shows up on your November scorecard. The fine itself often lands on the following month's remittance, so a November scorecard fine may not hit your check until late December or January. If your team measures deduction risk by remittance date rather than shipment date, the November miss looks like a January problem, and the root cause looks blurry.

faq.q: Why do returns deductions land in January instead of during the holiday?
faq.a: Retailers batch returns processing. Consumer returns from Black Friday and December sales sit in stores or reverse-logistics centers for weeks before they process against your account. Walmart returns codes 92, 93, and 94 typically show up on remittances 30 to 90 days after the Christmas peak. That is why the January remittance often runs materially larger than any month in Q4 itself. The volume is there, it is just not counted yet.

faq.q: Should I reserve dispute capacity for Q4, or spread it evenly?
faq.a: Do not spread it evenly. Endless Commerce reports dispute win rates of 75 to 80 percent when filed within seven days and 15 to 20 percent after 60 days. Your November OTIF fine hits your check in December. Your December shortage claim hits in January. Your January returns hit in February. If your dispute team is running at capacity through the peak, they miss the seven-day window on the exact deductions with the highest recovery odds. Staff the dispute window to the calendar, not to an average month.

faq.q: How large is a typical Q4 deduction cliff for a $50M CPG supplier?
faq.a: Deduction burden varies with retailer mix and program details, but a common pattern for a $50 million CPG supplier at a Walmart, Target, Amazon 1P, and Kroger mix: November through February deductions run 1.5 to 3 times the mid-year monthly average, driven by OTIF, shortage, and returns codes in sequence. That is $50,000 to $150,000 of additional exposure across the four-month window compared to a mid-year baseline, before any specific program change lands.

title: How to Read a Walmart Remittance and Spot the Disputes
description: Where the invoice number, PO number, and deduction code live on a Walmart remittance, and how to spot which lines are worth disputing.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram explaining how to read a Walmart remittance advice: the payment total, invoice reference block, and deduction code line labeled with arrows, plus a checklist equation for matching a code to a claim type
answer: A Walmart remittance advice is the payment document, an EDI 820, showing what was paid against each invoice and what was subtracted first. Deduction lines carry a numeric code, a dollar amount, and a reference back to the invoice or PO. Reading one means matching that code to a claim type, then deciding if the line is worth disputing.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 820 transaction-set structure (SPS Commerce's EDI reference), vendor guides to Walmart's Accounts Payable Dispute Portal and APIS search fields (SPS Commerce, iNymbus), and a 2025 industry benchmark on deduction write-off rates (Finortal, cited via OverDeduct), August 2026.

faq.q: Why is my Walmart check short?
faq.a: It's not a check for the invoice total. It's a check for the invoice total minus every deduction line Walmart's system applied first. Each deduction carries a code and a reason, and the check reflects the net after all of them.

faq.q: Where do I find what a Walmart deduction code means?
faq.a: The code itself appears on the remittance line, next to the amount and a reference back to the invoice or PO. What the code means isn't printed there. Look it up separately, in Walmart's own Retail Link documentation or a fact-checked reference like this site's deduction-code hub.

faq.q: Should I dispute every deduction on a Walmart remittance?
faq.a: No. Vendor sources point to frequency as the better signal, not size. One or two deductions in a cycle usually means a one-off error, worth a quick dispute. The same code every cycle points to a process problem upstream, worth fixing at the root.

faq.q: How long do I have to respond once I open a Walmart dispute?
faq.a: Per vendor documentation of the Accounts Payable Dispute Portal, a draft dispute expires automatically after 14 days if not submitted. A case Walmart marks 'Supplier Action' auto-closes if you don't respond within 7 days. The overall claim-dispute deadline for a given code is separate and varies. It isn't confirmed here.

title: The Five Amazon 1P Chargebacks That Cost Vendors Most
description: The five Amazon 1P chargeback categories that generate the most fees, what triggers each, the prevention step for each, and which you can still dispute.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Amazon 1P chargeback categories: PO on-time, ASN accuracy, carton labels, barcodes, and prep, each with a prevention step
answer: You reduce Amazon Vendor Central chargeback fees by fixing the root cause of each recurring defect, not by disputing charges one at a time. Five categories generate most of the money: PO On-Time Accuracy, ASN Accuracy, Carton Content Accuracy, Non-Compliant Barcode, and prep or packaging failures. Each is preventable before the shipment leaves your dock.
answerQualifier: Compiled from public vendor-compliance sources (SPS Commerce / SupplierWiki, Consulterce, iNymbus, RT7 Digital, SalesDuo, Endless Commerce, Amazowl), September 2026. Fee percentages and per-unit amounts are vendor-reported, vary by region and program update, and are flagged inline. Confirm the figure that applies to you in Vendor Central under Operational Performance.

faq.q: How much do Amazon vendor chargebacks cost?
faq.a: Vendor recovery firms report total chargeback exposure running as high as 5% of Amazon revenue, roughly $5,000 per $100,000, for vendors with unaddressed defects (SalesDuo). Individual fees vary by type: PO On-Time Accuracy is reported at 3% of product cost, rising to 10% for units never shipped (Amazowl, Consulterce). ASN Accuracy is reported at 2 to 6% of cost of goods (Consulterce). A case-pack barcode defect is reported at $26 per non-compliant unit (SPS Commerce). Your own Operational Performance report in Vendor Central has the figures that apply to your account.

faq.q: Can you dispute an Amazon vendor chargeback?
faq.a: Yes. Amazon gives you 30 days from the chargeback notification to dispute it in Vendor Central, and two dispute attempts per chargeback. Multiple vendor sources confirm both. RT7 Digital reports a roughly 70% success rate when the dispute includes a complete evidence set: EDI transmission logs, carrier proof of delivery, and appointment confirmations.

faq.q: What is the most common Amazon vendor chargeback?
faq.a: PO On-Time Accuracy and ASN Accuracy are the two categories vendors cite most often. PO On-Time Accuracy fires when confirmed units miss the delivery window. ASN Accuracy fires when the Advance Ship Notice does not match what the fulfillment center receives at the unit level. Both hit shipments that otherwise look clean.

faq.q: What is OTIF for Amazon vendors?
faq.a: OTIF means on-time, in-full. For Amazon 1P it maps to PO On-Time Accuracy: the units Amazon confirmed on the purchase order have to arrive inside the required window and match the confirmed quantity. A short shipment and a late shipment are measured separately, and a single delivery can fail both. See [what OTIF actually costs](/articles/what-is-otif.html).

faq.q: Does disputing a chargeback stop it from happening again?
faq.a: No. A dispute recovers one fee. It does nothing to the process that produced it. If your ERP builds the ASN from the order quantity instead of the confirmed pick, the next shipment carries the same defect and the same chargeback. Reducing the fee means changing where the data comes from, not winning the dispute.

title: The Six Documents You Need Before Disputing a Deduction
description: The six documents that turn a deduction dispute into a case: what each one proves, what it doesn't, and the order to pull them before the window closes.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Deduction evidence checklist: PO, pick ticket, ASN, BOL, POD, invoice, and retailer receipt linked in a chain
answer: A retail deduction evidence pack is the set of documents you assemble before filing a dispute: purchase order, pick ticket, EDI 856 ASN, bill of lading, proof of delivery, EDI 997 and 824 acknowledgments, invoice, and retailer receiving record. Each document proves one link in the chain. A POD proves the truck arrived. It doesn't prove the ASN was accepted or the invoice matched the PO. You need the full chain.
answerQualifier: Based on the public X12 EDI standard, SPS Commerce and Orderful supplier documentation, and Inmar and OverDeduct industry benchmarks, September 2026. Individual retailer dispute requirements vary by program.

faq.q: What documents do I need to dispute a retail deduction?
faq.a: You need the purchase order, pick ticket or warehouse shipment record, EDI 856 ASN, EDI 997 functional acknowledgment, EDI 824 application advice (if the retailer sends one), bill of lading, proof of delivery, invoice, and the retailer's own receiving record. Each proves one link. The gap between any two adjacent documents is where the deduction started.

faq.q: Does a proof of delivery prove a shortage deduction is wrong?
faq.a: A POD proves delivery happened. It doesn't prove the delivered quantity matched the ASN, the invoice, or the purchase order. A shortage deduction compares multiple quantities: ordered, picked, ASN'd, and received. The POD covers only one of those. You still need the other documents to show where the count diverged.

faq.q: Does a clean EDI 997 mean the retailer accepted my ASN?
faq.a: A 997 confirms the file parsed without syntax errors. It doesn't confirm the retailer accepted the business content, the quantities, the item identifiers, or the pack hierarchy. Business-level acceptance or rejection comes back on the EDI 824, if the retailer uses one. Treating the 997 as approval is one of the most common evidence gaps in deduction disputes.

faq.q: How long do I have to dispute a retail deduction?
faq.a: Dispute windows vary by retailer. Walmart uses multiple windows depending on claim type: up to 2 years from invoice date for general AP deductions, 12 months for shortage claims, and 15 to 30 days for AP chargebacks. Amazon gives 30 days with two dispute attempts. Target and Kroger each set their own windows by claim type. See our deduction dispute deadlines by retailer for the current reported windows.

title: You Shipped to the DC. Why Are Deductions Already Stacking Up?
description: In distribution does not mean retail-ready. The six operational gaps that turn a first retail PO into deductions, and how to close them before shipment.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Two side-by-side checklists comparing distribution-ready and retail-ready CPG supplier operations
answer: A CPG supplier is distribution-ready when it can ship product to a warehouse. It is retail-ready when every shipment meets a retailer's specific compliance rules for EDI, labeling, packaging, delivery windows, and invoicing. The gap between the two is where deductions start. Deductions run 5 to 15% of gross sales across the CPG sector, and most trace back to operational mismatches, not product defects. Closing the six gaps before the first PO ships is cheaper than disputing chargebacks after.
answerQualifier: Based on public vendor compliance documentation from Bravo CPG, SPS Commerce, Productiv, Inmar, and OverDeduct benchmarks, September 2026. Individual retailer compliance thresholds and penalty structures vary by program.

faq.q: What is the difference between distribution-ready and retail-ready?
faq.a: Distribution-ready means your product can reach a warehouse: you have packaging, a logistics partner, and a way to take orders. Retail-ready means every shipment meets the retailer's specific operational rules for EDI transmission, labeling format, packaging configuration, delivery timing, and invoicing accuracy. The difference is compliance, not capability.

faq.q: What percentage of revenue do CPG brands lose to retail deductions?
faq.a: Inmar reports that deductions account for 5 to 15% of gross sales in the CPG sector. For mid-market brands, Finortal's 2025 benchmark puts the write-off rate at 1.2 to 2.4% of gross revenue annually. On a $15M brand, that write-off alone is $180K to $360K per year.

faq.q: What are the most common retail compliance failures for new CPG suppliers?
faq.a: The most common failures are ASN accuracy mismatches between the advance ship notice and physical shipment, routing guide violations from not reading retailer-specific requirements, incomplete or incorrect labeling, missed delivery windows, and invoice discrepancies against the purchase order. Each failure generates its own chargeback category.

faq.q: How do I make my CPG brand retail-ready before the first PO?
faq.a: Map six areas before the first shipment: EDI capability and testing, GS1-128 labeling compliance, retailer-specific packaging configuration, delivery window and OTIF threshold awareness, invoice-to-PO matching rules, and a dispute process for when chargebacks arrive anyway. One person owning the weekly PO review reportedly reduces chargebacks without requiring infrastructure changes.

title: Retail Vendor Compliance: The Rulebook That Decides Your Margin
description: Retail vendor compliance is the routing-guide rulebook that turns a shipping, labeling, or EDI miss into a chargeback. What retailers grade, what it costs, and where to fix it.
author: Pixels and Clicks
pillarBlurb: The retailer rulebook: what gets graded, and how a single miss becomes a chargeback.
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard diagram showing a retailer routing guide, a shipment scanned at receiving, a flagged violation, and the resulting deduction on a remittance
answer: Retail vendor compliance is the set of rules a retailer publishes in its routing guide and vendor agreement covering how you ship, label, pack, and invoice. Break a rule and the retailer issues a chargeback, a deduction pulled off your payment, even when the product itself arrived complete and on time.
answerQualifier: Based on retailer compliance terms documented across this site's OTIF and EDI coverage, plus industry description from SPS Commerce, November 2026. Routing guides change without notice; confirm current terms in your own vendor portal.

faq.q: What is vendor compliance in retail?
faq.a: Vendor compliance is shipping to the specification a retailer publishes in its routing guide and vendor agreement: the delivery window, the pallet and carton configuration, the labels, the EDI documents, and the invoice format. Each retailer writes its own rulebook, so a supplier selling into Walmart, Target, Kroger, and Amazon manages four separate compliance programs at once.

faq.q: What is a vendor compliance chargeback?
faq.a: A chargeback is a deduction the retailer takes off your payment when a shipment breaks a routing-guide rule. It posts as a coded line on your remittance weeks after delivery. Unlike a product return, it has nothing to do with whether the goods were good. It is a fine for how the shipment or its paperwork failed to match the spec.

faq.q: How much do retail compliance chargebacks cost?
faq.a: Per-shipment penalties commonly run 1% to 5% of the affected invoice. Walmart applies 3% of cost of goods to non-compliant cases and Target applies 5% with a $150 minimum. Deduction-recovery vendors estimate the total drag at 2% to 5% of gross revenue across a supplier's book, and that 40% to 60% of the charges are preventable or invalid.

faq.q: What are the most common vendor compliance violations?
faq.a: The five domains retailers grade are EDI and ASN accuracy, on-time delivery, in-full quantity, labeling and carton configuration, and routing and packaging. Many of these trace back to a data or document mismatch in the ERP or EDI setup rather than anything that happened on the warehouse floor.

faq.q: How do you dispute a vendor compliance chargeback?
faq.a: Each retailer runs its own dispute portal and deadline clock, from Walmart's APDP in Retail Link to Amazon's Vendor Central. You need the shipment evidence, meaning the ASN, the bill of lading, and proof of delivery, filed before the window closes. The dispute deadline is the difference between a recoverable charge and a permanent one.

title: Retailer vs. Distributor Deductions: Which Ones Your Supply Chain Team Can Actually Fix
description: Both say 'shortage' on the remittance. One traces to your ASN, the other to a promotional agreement your broker negotiated. A sorting guide for CPG suppliers selling through both channels.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Two remittance printouts side by side labeled retailer and distributor with a small overlap circle below
answer: Retailer deductions trace to compliance scorecards, ASN discrepancies, and EDI failures you can diagnose from your own warehouse and shipping data. Distributor deductions trace to promotional agreements, manufacturer chargebacks, and trade-fund contracts that need a trade-promotion audit. The overlap is small: distributor fill-rate or labeling compliance fees that borrow retailer mechanics.
answerQualifier: Based on published supplier compliance documentation from SPS Commerce, SupplyPike/SupplierWiki, KeHE supplier policies, UNFI supplier compliance guides, and retailer program documentation from Walmart, Amazon, Target, and Kroger. October 2026.

faq.q: What is the difference between a retailer deduction and a distributor deduction?
faq.a: A retailer deduction comes from a retailer like Walmart or Amazon and references a compliance scorecard, a receiving count, or an EDI document. A distributor deduction comes from a distributor like KeHE or UNFI and references a promotional agreement, a manufacturer chargeback, a trade-fund contract, or a broker settlement. The backing documents, the dispute paths, and the specialists who resolve them are different.

faq.q: Can a distributor charge an OTIF-style fine?
faq.a: Yes. KeHE's GBB 2.0 scorecard weights fill rate at roughly 12.5 percent of the overall supplier grade, and UNFI charges a reported $250 fee for shipments arriving more than 30 minutes late. These are operational compliance fees that borrow the retailer's OTIF mechanics. They are the small overlap between the two categories.

faq.q: Does Pixels and Clicks diagnose distributor deductions?
faq.a: Pixels and Clicks diagnoses operational deductions that trace to your warehouse, your ASN, or your EDI configuration. Most distributor deductions trace to contracts, promotional agreements, and broker settlements instead. Pixels and Clicks can help with the narrow overlap: a distributor's fill-rate or labeling compliance fee that behaves like a retailer OTIF fine. For the rest, a trade-promotion management firm or a broker reconciliation team is the right specialist.

faq.q: What types of deductions does KeHE take from suppliers?
faq.a: KeHE groups its deductions into three categories: KeHE fees (MCB chargebacks, extra-performance fees, CONNECT BI allowances), unsaleables (underperforming, non-conforming, or spoiled product with a per-unit processing fee), and invoice adjustments. KeHE also charges an 8 percent fee on manufacturer chargebacks with a $65 per-DC minimum, per SPS Commerce.

faq.q: Should I use the same firm for retailer and distributor deduction recovery?
faq.a: Usually not. Retailer deductions need access to your warehouse management system, your EDI transaction history, and the retailer's compliance scorecard. Distributor deductions need access to the trade-promotion agreement, the broker's settlement reports, and the distributor's invoice detail. Different data, different resolution paths, different expertise.

title: Supplier Scorecard: How Retailers Grade You, and What a Bad Score Costs
description: A supplier scorecard is how a retailer grades your OTIF, fill rate, and ASN accuracy. What Walmart, Target, and Amazon measure, the thresholds that trigger review, and how a bad score becomes deductions.
author: Pixels and Clicks
pillarBlurb: How retailers grade you, and how a bad score turns into deductions and delisting.
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard diagram of a retailer supplier scorecard grading on-time delivery, fill rate, and ASN accuracy, with a low score flagging into review and deductions
answer: A supplier scorecard is the report card a retailer keeps on each vendor, grading on-time delivery, in-full fill rate, ASN and EDI accuracy, and compliance. Walmart, Target, and Amazon each run their own version. A low score triggers review, fines, and eventually delisting, so the scorecard is the leading indicator of a supplier's deduction risk.
answerQualifier: Based on retailer scorecard metrics documented across this site's OTIF, fill-rate, and ASN coverage, November 2026. Each retailer sets its own thresholds and changes them; confirm current terms in your own vendor portal.

faq.q: What is a supplier scorecard?
faq.a: A supplier scorecard, also called a vendor scorecard, is how a retailer measures a vendor's performance over time. It grades delivery, fill rate, documentation accuracy, and compliance, usually against a target the retailer sets. The score drives whether you keep favorable terms, land on a corrective-action plan, or face review and deductions, so it is the retailer's single clearest signal of how you are doing as a supplier.

faq.q: What metrics are on a supplier scorecard?
faq.a: The core metrics are on-time delivery, in-full fill rate, and ASN or EDI accuracy, often rolled up as OTIF. Retailers add compliance measures for labeling, routing, and packaging, and some include quality and invoice accuracy. On-time and in-full usually carry the most weight, because they predict whether the shelf gets filled when the retailer expects it.

faq.q: What is a good supplier scorecard score?
faq.a: It depends on the retailer's own threshold, and the bar is high: fill-rate and on-time targets in the high nineties are common, and falling below the line triggers fines rather than a warning. The practical read is simpler than the exact number. A score trending down is an early signal of deductions coming, and a score below the retailer's threshold means they are already posting.

faq.q: What is the Walmart supplier scorecard?
faq.a: Walmart grades suppliers on OTIF, the on-time and in-full standard enforced through its fine program, visible to vendors in Retail Link. It is one example of the pattern every major retailer follows: a measured target, a penalty for missing it, and a portal where the score lives. Target and Amazon run comparable scorecards with their own metrics and thresholds.

faq.q: How do you improve a supplier scorecard?
faq.a: Work the metric that carries the most weight first, usually on-time-in-full, then ASN accuracy. Most scorecard misses are not warehouse failures; they trace to a data or document gap between the ASN, the invoice, and the physical shipment. Closing that gap in the ERP and EDI setup lifts the score and cuts the deductions that follow from it at the same time.

title: Target Vendor Chargebacks: What Each VC Code Costs
description: Target tracks violations, not AP codes like Walmart. What each VC violation type costs, how the VC prefix works, and how to dispute one.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Target retail vendor chargeback guide
answer: Target doesn't deduct by a single AP code list like Walmart. It tracks compliance violations, such as late shipping, missed fill rate, or ASN errors, and converts an unexempted one into a coded chargeback (prefix VC) after two weeks. Vendor sources disagree on the exact percentage charged, but agree on the mechanism and the Synergy dispute path.
answerQualifier: Compiled from five independent public vendor sources (SPS Commerce, iNymbus, Distribution Alternatives, WarehouseQuote, Productiv), August 2026. Penalty percentages conflict between sources and are flagged inline. Confirm the exact rate for your violation against your own Partners Online chargeback detail.

faq.q: What does the VC code on a Target chargeback mean?
faq.a: VC stands for Vendor Compliance, per iNymbus's deduction-prefix guide. It covers on-time shipping, pickup adherence, fill rate, and ASN availability. SPS Commerce separately describes filing a dispute "by VC number," which lines up with iNymbus's table. If your remittance shows a different prefix, it likely falls under CB (invoice-match), TRT (freight), RTVS (returns), or VIAP/VONL (vendor income) instead.

faq.q: How much does a Target compliance violation cost?
faq.a: Vendor sources disagree. Distribution Alternatives reports a flat 5% of cost of goods with a $150 minimum across on-time and fill-rate violations. WarehouseQuote reports a tiered structure instead: 1.5% for a general performance-adherence miss, 3% for on-time collect, on-time prepaid, and fill-rate-original violations. Confirm the rate on your own chargeback detail in Partners Online.

faq.q: What's the difference between a Target violation and a chargeback?
faq.a: A violation is a system-generated flag, not yet a deduction. Per SPS Commerce, it stays open for two weeks, during which a supplier can request an exemption if the violation is invalid. If it goes unexempted through that window, it converts to a chargeback and comes off the next payment.

faq.q: How do I dispute a Target vendor chargeback?
faq.a: Through the Synergy Vendor Dispute app inside the Partners Online (POL) portal, per SPS Commerce. Disputes are filed individually by VC number with supporting documentation, such as a proof of delivery, bill of lading, or screenshot. SupplyPike's help documentation separately reports a roughly 90-day dispute window for compliance chargebacks.

faq.q: How is Target's chargeback system different from Walmart's?
faq.a: Walmart deducts directly against a remittance line, coded to one of a fixed set of AP codes like 22 or 25. Target's compliance program works as a two-step pipeline instead. A violation posts first, and a supplier can get it exempted. Only an unexempted violation converts into a coded chargeback. The dispute portals, the code prefixes, and even the vocabulary differ between the two retailers.

title: From Vendor Central to Seller Central: What Actually Changes
description: The operational shift from Amazon 1P to 3P: what changes in ordering, fees, pricing control, and margin when you move from Vendor Central to Seller Central.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Side-by-side comparison of Amazon Vendor Central and Seller Central flows showing purchase orders versus direct listings
answer: Moving from Vendor Central to Seller Central replaces Amazon's wholesale purchase-order model with a direct listing model. You gain pricing control and 14-day payment cycles but take on inventory risk, advertising spend, and per-unit FBA fees. Gross margin per unit is usually higher on 3P. Net margin depends on your referral rate, FBA tier, and ad spend.
answerQualifier: Based on Amazon's published fee schedules, Jungle Scout marketplace research, vendor community experience on r/VendorCentral, and industry reporting from SupplyKick and Mars United on Amazon's Vendor Central termination waves. October 2026.

faq.q: Can I keep my ASINs when moving from Vendor Central to Seller Central?
faq.a: Your ASINs stay. They belong to the Amazon catalog, not to your seller or vendor account. You create Seller Central offers against the same ASINs. The product detail pages, reviews, and sales rank carry over. What changes is who owns the Buy Box listing. Your 3P offer competes with every other seller on the same ASIN, including Amazon itself if they still hold inventory.

faq.q: Is selling on Amazon more profitable as 1P or 3P?
faq.a: Gross margin per unit is typically higher on 3P because you set the retail price and pay a percentage referral fee instead of accepting a wholesale discount. Net margin depends on your category's referral rate, your average selling price, FBA fees per unit, advertising spend, and return rate. Low-ASP products with heavy FBA fees can net less on 3P than on 1P.

faq.q: Can I sell on both Vendor Central and Seller Central at the same time?
faq.a: Yes. Many brands run a hybrid model. They keep high-volume SKUs on Vendor Central where Amazon's purchase orders provide predictable volume and list long-tail or higher-margin SKUs on Seller Central for pricing control. The risk is that Amazon's 1P offer on the same ASIN usually wins the Featured Offer, which limits your 3P sales on overlapping products.

faq.q: How long does it take to transition from Vendor Central to Seller Central?
faq.a: A basic Seller Central account setup takes a few days. Building the operational infrastructure to manage listings, FBA shipments, advertising, and customer service takes 60 to 90 days for most brands. Plan for a gap period where sales volume drops while your 3P listings build ranking and advertising momentum.

faq.q: What fees does Amazon charge on Seller Central vs Vendor Central?
faq.a: Seller Central charges a per-unit referral fee (typically 15% of the sale price), FBA fulfillment fees (starting at $3.65 for the smallest standard-size items), monthly storage fees, and optional advertising costs. Vendor Central takes a wholesale discount (typically 40 to 60% off retail), plus chargebacks for compliance failures, plus co-op and marketing allowances. The fee structures are completely different.

title: The Walmart OTIF Fine, the 3% Rate, and What Drives a Miss
description: Walmart's OTIF fine is a program-level chargeback, not a per-shipment dispute. Current thresholds, how the 3% rate applies, and what drives a miss.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram explaining Walmart's OTIF fine: a delivery truck against a clock and a percentage sign labeled 3%, with a checklist equation showing on-time plus in-full compliance versus a chargeback
answer: Walmart's OTIF fine is a program-level chargeback: 3% of the cost of goods on cases that miss the on-time or in-full window, not a per-shipment claim like a deduction code. Since February 2024, prepaid suppliers need 90% on-time and 95% in-full, and collect suppliers need 98% collect-ready. That's down from a unified 98% requirement in place since 2020.
answerQualifier: Fact-checked against named trade-press reporting, not Walmart's own documentation. Walmart announced this change via the gated Retail Link portal only, with no public press release. Percentages and effective date current as of August 2026. Retailer programs change without notice.

faq.q: Is the OTIF fine the same thing as a deduction code like Walmart code 24?
faq.a: No. A deduction code like code 24 disputes a specific shipment's counted quantity. It's tied to one PO. The OTIF fine is a program-level chargeback calculated from your aggregate on-time and in-full rate across a measurement period. There's no single code number to look up on a remittance.

faq.q: Is the 3% rate applied to all of my shipments, or just the ones that miss?
faq.a: Just the non-compliant cases. The 3% chargeback applies to the value of cases that missed the on-time or in-full threshold, not your total shipment value. That's part of why reported aggregate fine burden across suppliers runs far below the headline 3% rate: roughly 0.16% of cost of goods sold, per Uber Freight data cited by Forbes.

faq.q: Do prepaid and collect suppliers have the same OTIF targets?
faq.a: No. Prepaid suppliers, who arrange their own freight, are held to a 90% on-time target measured against the Must Arrive By Date. Collect suppliers, where Walmart arranges freight, are measured on a 98% collect-ready standard instead. Both supplier types share the same 95% in-full target.

faq.q: Why did Walmart lower the OTIF threshold from 98% in 2024?
faq.a: Walmart hasn't published its own reasoning publicly. The change was announced through the Retail Link supplier portal rather than a press release. Public reporting frames it as splitting one blended 98% target into two separate, more specific metrics, on-time and in-full, rather than a straightforward loosening of the bar.

title: What Is OTIF? On-Time-In-Full Explained
description: OTIF measures whether a supplier delivered the full quantity inside the retailer's window. How retailers calculate it, and what a miss costs.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard-style diagram explaining OTIF: stacked delivery boxes labeled On Time (Schedule), In Full (Quality), and Accurate (Details), with a checklist equation showing on-time plus in-full equals OTIF success
answer: OTIF stands for On-Time-In-Full. It is the metric major retailers use to measure whether a supplier delivered the correct quantity (in-full) within the agreed delivery window (on-time). Walmart, Target, Kroger, and Amazon each run their own version, with penalty rates between 1% and 5% of cost of goods on non-compliant shipments.
answerQualifier: Based on publicly reported retailer thresholds (Forbes/Steve Banker for Walmart, vendor compliance documentation for Target, WarehouseQuote for Kroger, Front Row Group and Commerce Canal for Amazon), a McKinsey/Trading Partner Alliance out-of-stock study, and FourKites/Supply Chain Dive coverage of Kraft Heinz's OTIF improvement initiative, August 2026. Retailer programs change without notice; confirm current thresholds in your own portal.

faq.q: What does OTIF stand for?
faq.a: On-Time-In-Full. It is a compound metric: the on-time rate measures whether shipments arrived within the retailer's delivery window, and the in-full rate measures whether the shipped quantity matched the purchase order. Most retailers track and penalize these two components separately.

faq.q: What is a good OTIF score?
faq.a: Above 95% is generally considered acceptable by most major retailers. Walmart requires 90% on-time and 95% in-full for prepaid suppliers. Target fines any unit outside the ship window and expects a 95% fill rate. The top quartile of CPG suppliers typically runs above 97%, according to industry benchmarks.

faq.q: Is OTIF the same as fill rate?
faq.a: No. Fill rate measures only the quantity dimension: what percentage of ordered units you shipped. OTIF adds the time dimension. A shipment that arrives complete but two days late has a 100% fill rate and a 0% on-time rate. Retailers penalize both.

faq.q: How are OTIF fines calculated?
faq.a: Each retailer applies a percentage of cost of goods (COGS) to non-compliant cases. Walmart charges 3% on cases that miss. Target charges 5%. Kroger starts at 1% of invoice value or $250 per order, whichever is greater. The fine applies only to the non-compliant portion, not your total shipment value.

faq.q: Do all retailers measure OTIF the same way?
faq.a: No. They agree on the concept but differ on every operational detail: what counts as the delivery window, whether it's measured at the case or PO level, how the in-full threshold works, and what the penalty rate is. A supplier shipping to all four major US retailers manages four different compliance programs.

title: When the Deduction on Your Remittance Isn't an Ops Problem
description: Four deduction families trace to contracts, not operations. Three trace to your warehouse and your data. One question on a remittance line tells you which is which.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Stick figure at a fork in the road holding a remittance printout, left path labeled ops problem and right path labeled contract problem
answer: Seven deduction families appear on a CPG remittance. Four of them, promo billback, trade-fund and MDF, price-protection and holdback, and slotting and co-op, trace to a contract your sales team signed. Three of them, OTIF and compliance, ASN and shortage, and EDI and data-integrity, trace to your warehouse, your shipping data, or your EDI configuration. The sorting question is whether the deduction references a compliance scorecard or a contractual clause.
answerQualifier: Based on McKinsey and Forrester research on CPG trade-promotion spending, retailer compliance documentation from Walmart, Amazon, Kroger, and Target, and published deduction-resolution practitioner guidance. October 2026.

faq.q: How do I tell whether a deduction on my remittance is a contract problem or an operations problem?
faq.a: Pull the reason code and the backing document from the remittance line. If the code references a promo fund, an MDF agreement, a price-protection clause, or a slotting fee, the deduction traces to a contract your sales or trade-marketing team negotiated. If it references an OTIF scorecard, an ASN discrepancy, a shortage count, or an EDI rejection, it traces to your warehouse or your data. The first group needs a trade-promotion auditor or a broker. The second group needs an operational diagnostic.

faq.q: What deduction types does a diagnostic firm like Pixels and Clicks not cover?
faq.a: Pixels and Clicks does not diagnose promo billback, trade-fund or MDF deductions, price-protection or holdback chargebacks, or slotting and co-op fees. All four trace to a contract, not to a shipping or data failure. The specialists for those are trade-promotion management firms, broker reconciliation teams, and pricing-dispute counsel.

faq.q: What percentage of CPG revenue goes to trade-promotion deductions?
faq.a: CPG manufacturers spend roughly 20 percent of gross revenue on trade promotion, per McKinsey and Forrester research, with some categories running as high as 25 percent. The bulk of that spend flows through promo billback and trade-fund mechanisms, which are contract-driven and outside the scope of an operational deduction diagnostic.

faq.q: What deduction types trace to warehouse or shipping data problems?
faq.a: Three families trace to operations. OTIF and compliance deductions come from missed delivery windows or failed scorecard thresholds. ASN and shortage deductions come from what the retailer counted versus what your ASN declared. EDI and data-integrity deductions come from rejected or mismatched electronic documents like the 856, 810, or 997. All three are diagnosable from your own shipping records, ASN logs, and EDI transaction history.

faq.q: Should I hire one firm to handle all my retail deductions?
faq.a: Probably not. Contract-driven deductions require access to the trade-promotion agreement and the broker's records. Operational deductions require access to your warehouse management system, your EDI logs, and the retailer's compliance scorecard. The skill sets, the data sources, and the resolution paths are different. Hiring one firm for both usually means one side gets the B team.

title: Why Growing With Walmart Can Shrink Your Margin
description: The price on your Walmart PO is gross, not net. Trade promotions, deductions, fees, and a 68-day cash gap can turn rising sales into a shrinking margin, and some accounts into a loss.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Hand-drawn whiteboard diagram of a Walmart dollar shrinking through trade spend, deductions, fees, and a cash gap into net margin
answer: Growing with Walmart can shrink your margin because the purchase order price is gross, not net. Trade promotions, deductions and compliance fines, fees, and a long cash gap each take a cut before the money reaches your bank. Scale them far enough and an account can grow while it loses money.
answerQualifier: Based on Pixels and Clicks analysis of SEC 10-K filings, a Nielsen trade-promotion review reported by FoodNavigator, and Pixels and Clicks research pages. November 2026.

faq.q: What is the gross-to-net gap for CPG brands?
faq.a: The gross-to-net gap is the difference between a product's list or PO price and the revenue a brand keeps. Trade promotions, retailer deductions and compliance fines, contractual fees, and the cash tied up before a retailer pays each reduce the gross number. On a CPG income statement, the result is reported as net sales.

faq.q: Why does revenue grow faster than profit at a CPG brand?
faq.a: Revenue often grows faster than profit because the cuts between gross and net scale with volume. More units mean more trade spend funded, more shipments exposed to deductions and OTIF fines, and more cash tied up waiting for payment. A bigger retail account multiplies all three at once, so net margin can stay flat while gross sales climb.

faq.q: Why do most trade promotions lose money?
faq.a: In a review of 39 million US promotional events, almost three-quarters did not break even, per Nielsen as reported by FoodNavigator. A promotion that costs more in discount and funding than it returns in extra units is a loss. Run enough of them through one account and its growth can stop paying for itself.

faq.q: What is a negative run rate on a retail account?
faq.a: A negative run rate is when extra volume through an account adds revenue but subtracts margin. Each incremental promoted case carries the full stack of trade spend, deductions, fees, and cash carry. Past a point, the next case clears less than it costs, so the account grows and loses money at the same time.

faq.q: Which part of the gross-to-net gap can a supplier recover?
faq.a: Trade terms, fees, and payment days move only when a supplier renegotiates with the buyer. Disputed deductions are the exception. A deduction a retailer took in error is cash it already holds, and each one traces to a cause in the ASN, the invoice, or the item file. Those are recoverable without changing the contract.

title: Why Amazon Deducts After Your ERP Migration
description: Two weeks after ERP go-live, Amazon deducts on shipments you sent complete. The cases scanned fine. The unit UPCs did not. What broke, and how to catch it.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: The four item-master barcode fields a NetSuite or Business Central migration can map wrong: primary UPC, additional barcode, item alias GTIN, and unit-of-measure item reference
answer: After an ERP migration, your cases can ship with the correct case label but the wrong unit-level UPC. Amazon's fulfillment center scans the unit. If the scan resolves to a different item than your ASN declared, Amazon posts a shortage on your ASIN and an overage on the mystery item. The remittance signature: a matched shortage and overage on the same PO.
answerQualifier: Based on Oracle NetSuite's own help documentation (UPC Code field, item aliases, GTIN 01 identifier), Microsoft Learn's Business Central item-reference documentation, public GS1 and Amazon barcode-requirement guidance, and a pattern that supplier operators have described publicly on r/VendorCentral (linked in the piece). September 2026.

faq.q: Why does a shortage claim show up when the shipment left complete?
faq.a: Amazon's fulfillment center scans at the unit level, not just the case. If the case label scans to the correct ASIN but the unit label inside scans to a different real ASIN, Amazon books zero receipt on your item and an unexpected receipt on the mystery item. The first is a shortage. The second is an overage. Both hit the same PO.

faq.q: Why did our cutover UAT pass without catching a wrong UPC?
faq.a: UAT test data is usually seeded with UPCs the test scripts already know are correct. Nothing in the test compares the new item master against physical labels on inventory produced under the old master. The mismatch only surfaces when Amazon scans real pre-cutover inventory against the new master's expectation of what the label should be.

faq.q: Which item-master field usually breaks in a NetSuite or Business Central migration?
faq.a: The field that stores the scannable identifier at the unit of measure Amazon actually receives. In NetSuite, that is the UPC Code on the item record or a GTIN in the item aliases table. In Business Central, that is an Item Reference of type Barcode tied to the correct unit of measure. A migration that maps the each-level UPC to the case-level record, or the reverse, ships product whose labels do not match the item master.

faq.q: How do I catch this at pallet scan instead of after the deduction lands?
faq.a: Before the pallet leaves the dock, scan one unit-level barcode. Look up the value in your ERP's item-reference or alias table. Compare the result against the item the ASN is about to declare for that PO. If they do not match, block the ASN. NetSuite item aliases and Business Central item references both support this lookup natively.

faq.q: How do I tell a UPC-migration failure apart from a real shortage?
faq.a: A physical shortage shows up as one line: units expected, units received short. A UPC-migration failure shows up as two lines on the same PO: a shortage line for your ASIN and an unexpected-item overage line for a different ASIN at the same case count. The matched pair is the signature.

title: Your Team After AI: What Most Agencies Never Plan For
description: Most AI agencies sell a deployment. The harder question is what happens to your team and your workflows after the system goes live. That determines whether the project works or gets abandoned.
author: Pixels and Clicks
imageAlt: Stick figure at a crossroads between unused tool and team upgrade, with a workflow chart and upward arrow
answer: AI implementation succeeds or fails based on what happens to your team after the system goes live. The automation has to target the real bottleneck, freed capacity has to be redeployed to higher-value work, and the team has to adopt the new workflow. Most agencies plan for the first. Almost none plan for the other two.
answerQualifier: Based on the working methodology of Pixels and Clicks, Gartner research on GenAI project abandonment (2024), and McKinsey data on transformation program outcomes. October 2026.

faq.q: How does Pixels and Clicks approach AI implementation differently from other agencies?
faq.a: Pixels and Clicks starts with a paid assessment that maps how work actually gets done before proposing any build. The assessment deliverable is a process map showing every step the team takes, the time each step costs, and where the gaps are between what leadership described and what operations does. The assessment also includes a go/no-go recommendation.

faq.q: Does Pixels and Clicks replace employees with AI?
faq.a: Pixels and Clicks automates low-value repetitive work so existing employees can move to higher-value tasks like deduction tracing, dispute management, and root-cause analysis. Every engagement includes a redeployment plan that names the specific higher-value work and sequences it by priority.

faq.q: What are the first, second, and third order effects of AI implementation?
faq.a: First order: the automated task gets faster and more accurate. Second order: the person who did that task moves to judgment-heavy work that compounds value. Third order: the organization starts questioning inefficiencies it used to accept as cost of doing business.

faq.q: Why does Pixels and Clicks run a paid assessment before building anything?
faq.a: The real bottleneck rarely matches what leadership describes. Building an automation from a description of the workflow rather than mapping how the team actually works produces tools the team ignores. The assessment maps the real process and costs before any build decision. We've walked away from paid build work after an assessment showed the manual process cost less than the automation would.

faq.q: What does change management look like in a Pixels and Clicks engagement?
faq.a: Every automated workflow gets a named owner inside the company, picked during the build. The workflow ships with a one-page runbook covering what the system does, what it replaced, what to check when something looks wrong, and who to call. Walkthroughs are live calls. Training runs alongside the build.
